We have conducted extensive experiments utilizing this methodology for language generation, machine translation, and summarization, achieving notable improvements of up to 15% in terms of BLEU score compared to both individual methods and a range of alternative integrated techniques.

Laurent polynomials that represent tropicalizations of Fano varieties from a specific mutation class share a significant property - they have an equivalent divisor representation across all their Knevck forms. By establishing this fact, we demonstrate that these Laurent polynomials are closely linked to the tropicalization of Hodge bundles over their associated parameter space. As a result, we show that the mutation classes of Laurent polynomials that correspond to abelian varieties or K3 surfaces have a connection to Picard groups of simplicity, reflecting a deeper relationship between these varieties and their geometric representations.

Reconstructing a three-dimensional face from multiple views is a complex task because the same face can be observed from infinite angles.  However, not all views are equally common.  For example, profiles are typically seen more often than the side view.  This problem becomes even more challenging when considering both the shape and position of the face.  In our proposed approach, a Self-Aligned Dual Face Regression Network is used to create a 3D face from both pose-dependent and pose-independent factors.  We generate a realistic face when given a single image, such as an eye, but we achieve more accurate results when given more information, such as a single view of the face but its orientation.  Our method produces high-quality results, outperforming the current state-of-the-art techniques, demonstrating its effectiveness through both quantitative and qualitative evaluations.

We investigated a two-dimensional SU($N$) lattice model with a finite charge density to determine how it affects the mobility of fractons, which are particles that cannot move freely due to constraints imposed by the symmetry of the system. Despite the presence of a finite charge density, we found that the fracton gap persists and the mobility of the Kitaev spin liquid model can be modified by adjusting the symmetry-breaking parameter, which may be useful for controllable manipulation of the fractons in this region. Furthermore, we discovered that the model can support both bosonic and fermionic fractons, as well as monopoles, and that the monopole constraint is only prevented when the charge density is exactly zero.

A notable feature of the CMB is the large, negative region in the Bardeen potential observed at a specific angular scale. We investigate the possibility that this anomaly could be linked to the scalar power spectrum of the primordial fluctuations. To achieve the desired potential values, the power spectrum would need to be around 1.5 times the currently accepted value. We explore the potential for certain inflationary models to produce such a power spectrum while maintaining consistency with existing observational constraints. The model that shows the most promise is the $\phi$-symmetric inflation potential, which exhibits a local amplitude for the Bardeen potential that is in line with the conditions necessary to replicate the $l=140$ multipole anomaly observed in the CMB. The likelihood of replicating the observed Bardeen potential spectrum with sufficient precision using finite samples of theoretical models is reported as a measure of the relevance of this model.

Researchers examine the structure of trees with a standard ordering, specifically ordered trees with no repeated edges, where the root has a specific rank. They explore the number of deepest nodes in these trees, counting only standard ordered trees up to 8 ranks and marking specific nodes. The focus on standard ordering raises a question about the number of deepest nodes in general ordered trees, prompting further study. A distinction is drawn between rooted ordered trees, where the ordering matters, and general ordered trees, where it does not. An existing approach to counting general ordered trees is reviewed by counting the number of deepest nodes in rooted ordered trees. By contrast, the number of deepest nodes is shown to be uniform at 1 for all marked ordered trees. The same uniformity is displayed for trees with the root at the deepest level, making the same distinction between rooted and general ordered trees. The distribution of the kth deepest node was calculated for all marked ordered trees, with values ranging from 1 to the root rank. The distribution is modeled using a modified version of the Yule-Simon effect, with results showing that the effect holds for the kth deepest node when k is greater than 2.

In the context of automated vote tabulation, the combination of optical character recognition and spell correction can enhance the accuracy of this process. We developed a specialized spell correction algorithm that adapts standard techniques to address the unique characteristics of scanned ballots containing hand-written votes. This tailored approach leverages a database of correctly transcribed sample ballots to inform the correction process and improve the likelihood of valid outcomes. We evaluated the efficacy of our method on a diverse set of real-world ballot images and found that it effectively corrected inaccuracies introduced by optical character recognition, yielding an notable reduction in errors. Notably, our work is distinct from other spell correction applications, where the goal is to correct misspelled words likely stemming from pronunciation or other sources, in contrast to our scenario where the optical character recognition system can in some cases be perfect, but sometimes falls short due to the inherent difficulties in scanning hand-written materials, a challenge our work addresses with relative simplicity.

In the training of modern linear models, data often extends infinitely in one direction. Despite this, traditional techniques for stratified sampling can lead to biased estimates if used directly. The issue becomes even more complex when models are made neural. The problem gets even more challenging when there are infinite dimensions in multiple directions. The paper presents an innovative way to reduce the infinite dimensionality of data by using a sampling method that combines stochastic approximation and iterative mining. The proposed technique is applicable to both over-parameterized linear models and neural networks. The paper shows that the new method yields accurate and unbiased estimates of infinite-dimensional data. The proposed method is particularly effective when there are time-dependent variables in the data. The paper also includes the theoretical proof that the proposed method achieves the optimal rate of convergence. The new technique is tested on synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.

Recent work utilizing a bidirectional attention-based architecture at both the encoder and decoder levels has achieved notable success in low-variance code mixing (LCM) speech separation. To further explore the potential of this approach, we propose a cooperative bidirectional attention architecture (CBAA) that incorporates a cooperative mechanism between encoders and cross-domain attention between spectograms and magnitude spectra. In our experiments, CBAA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, including the bidirectional attention-based architecture, on both male-male speech separation and real-world data speeches. Notably, CBAA achieved a significant improvement of 0.31 in the short-time objective intelligibility (STOI) score and 0.26 in the reduced equivalent background noise (RBGN) score without background noise on the male-male dataset, and a high score of 0.794 in both cases on the female-female dataset. Moreover, CBAA demonstrated superior speech quality and robustness when dealing with recordings with background noises, particularly in the case of female speakers.

The fundamental function of pressure and temperature sensors in an aircraft's Normal Power Plant (NPP) is to provide accurate data to the flight control system. Any manipulation of these sensors could have serious consequences for the safety of the aircraft. This research paper presents an original idea for compromising differential pressure sensors (DPSs) in an NPP by deliberately introducing an electrical interference, which would result in an unauthorized change in the aircraft's altitude. Furthermore, this proposed interference could potentially affect other aircraft systems that utilize similar sensor technologies. To mitigate this threat, a method of protection is suggested that utilizes a method of protection inspired by the human brain's neural networks. This proposed protection method was evaluated using a simulation tool, which showed promising results in preventing the DPSs from being compromised under various forms of electrical interference.

As the transition to a carbon-neutral energy system progresses, it's essential to model future energy storage resources with a mindset of managing risks rather than solely optimizing economic benefits. We begin by illustrating how a single player approaches storage management under various risk preferences, including Kovalev's model, which ensures against a specified probability of economic losses exceeding a certain threshold. We then integrate this individual optimization with a mean-field game theory to find a storage equilibrium that can be incorporated into a general LRP (Chance-Constrained Linear Program). Finally, we apply this storage model to a local electricity market, incorporating generators and demand sources with their own risk management strategies, and examine how different storage risk preferences influence the market's equilibrium.

To study core-excited states at the Cu K-edge in Cu(100)-c(2x2)Au adlayers, a novel solid-state source with adjustable energy was used.  By matching the energy of x-ray pulses to specific energy differences between states, researchers induced coherent electron motion between these states and gathered data using scanning tunneling spectroscopy.  Two routes to state-to-state dynamics were identified - direct excitation, where the initial state directly leads to a state of lower energy, and indirect, where the initial state first decomposes into two states, with one then driving the system towards the lower-energy state.  Adjusting the photon energy allowed for control over these routes and their associated timescales.  The results show that in some cases, the initial decomposition of the excited state occurs in a matter of femtoseconds, while in other instances, this step takes longer and may be influenced by the availability of screening channels.  The research demonstrates the capability to systematically investigate core-excited states and their dynamics through a combination of x-ray absorption near edge spectroscopy and scanning tunneling spectroscopy, enabled by a high-fluctuation x-ray free-electron laser.

Our research analyzed the atmosphere of Mars using a general circulation model, with conditions similar to those of pre-industrial Earth. The simulation included volcanic aerosols in the atmosphere, with the same level of distribution as observed during the Mars Science Laboratory era. Despite the differences, the model successfully replicated the baroclinic storm patterns found on Mars. These storms displayed the same characteristic swirls and global circulation patterns as the circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere. The model showed that the atmosphere of Mars was home to mid-latitude storm systems that shifted seasons, permanent polar vortices, and massive dust storm events that could last from days to several solar days. The model also revealed the intricate dance of atmospheric mass, the movement of atmospheric winds, and the flow of atmospheric heat across the planet. The most striking feature of the model was the massive dust storm that developed in the summer, covering nearly half of the planet, and showed that this storm was driven by a collapse of pressure differences caused by the warming of the planet.

Current active learning methodologies, which adapt no-label pre-trained models to query the most informative samples, often excel on smaller benchmark datasets but significantly underperform when applied to large datasets like ImageNet. This paper argues that this failure stems from the lack of a clear distinction between true positive and negative classes, which is a crucial issue when dealing with large datasets. It proposes a new framework called Diversity-Accuracy Trade-Off (DATA) that actively balances the reduction of unknown classes while maximizing the margin between known classes, thereby enhancing the overall model performance. This approach is showcased by successfully applying DATA to the QuoVae framework and the large-scale ImageNet dataset, achieving notable improvements of up to 11.4% top-1 accuracy compared to conventional active learning strategies.

Researchers have been attempting to define a comprehensive algebraic multiplicity concept, capable of distinguishing the dynamics surrounding a stable equilibrium point, such as a rotating equilibrium in the duffing oscillator, and a Hopf bifurcation in the van der Pol oscillator. The Schur operator, used to analyze non-smooth near-equilibrium dynamics in the planar area preserving maps, has been found to be a reliable indicator of this phenomenon. The study introduces the generalized algebraic multiplicity (gam) of a map at a given point by extending the concept of the Schur operator, and demonstrates its effectiveness through successful classification and visualization methods. The proposed approach simplifies the process of identifying and distinguishing different equilibrium types, including those with multiple Floquet multipliers located at the Guckenheimer-Holmes point in the parameter space. The new approach is particularly valuable for non-smooth maps, and the term "algebraic multiplicity" is now more accurately referred to as "generalized algebraic multiplicity".

We investigate a variable-length cavity containing a single-mode pump beam and two entangled photon fields, which can generate two-mode squeezing. Our model accounts for loss in two areas and also includes the impact of a phase angle on the observing quantum fields. Initially, we determine the optimal length of the cavity that produces the greatest two-mode squeezing. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this phenomenon can enhance sensing of an optical phase and estimate the associated Heisenberg-limited phase shift per unit of phase angle. Additionally, we explore different initial states, including single-mode states and other two-mode states, and show that some of these states can achieve the same level of sensitivity in phase sensing. Finally, we propose an experimental approach using existing resources to implement this phenomenon.

Achieving high fidelity and controlled operation of quantum gates is crucial for the development and operation of scalable quantum computing systems. In silicon quantum electronics, employing valley-valve operations and coupled qubits provides a viable approach for the implementation of two-qubit gates. However, the functionality of these gates relies on the manipulation of electron spin, which is susceptible to spin-orbit interactions and thus subject to dissipation. Utilizing tight-binding model parameters, we investigate how placing donor atoms near the qubit sites influences the performance of two-qubit gates, specifically the molecular and hyperfine interactions, and find that strategically positioning these atoms can enhance the gate's accuracy. Furthermore, we identify an optimal placement that minimizes the disruption of the valley states and maximize the effectiveness of the two-qubit gate, and demonstrate the capacity to precision-tune the gate's operation through positioning alone.

In our investigation, we observed significant resistance fluctuations near the zero Landau level in large semiconductor samples, and our findings indicated that these resistance oscillations are driven by the scattering of electrons within the quantum well. The interplay between the two primary scattering mechanisms in the quantum well allowed us to develop a comprehensive understanding of the counter-intuitive behavior seen in the resistance oscillations. The presence of a substantial spin splitting caused by the large magnetic field led to a redistribution of the electrons across different Landfill levels, resulting in distinct resistance fluctuations near the zero Landfill level as a result of an electron spin-driven scattering process. The scattering of electrons within the same orbital but opposite spin states also contributed significantly to the resistance fluctuations observed in the very low carrier density samples. The study of the spin splitting and its influence on the resistance fluctuations may provide valuable insights into the development of highly sensitive magnetic field sensors. The design of such sensors could utilize a thin quantum well with a low carrier concentration, made from extrinsic semiconductors with a small energy gap, such as Al$_{0.82}$Ga$_{0.18}$As, where the spin splitting is sufficiently large to give a significant response over several resistance oscillations near the zero Landfill level.

This research paper proposes an adaptive cooperative nonorthogonal multiple access (AC-NOMA) protocol that dynamically selects between cooperative and noncooperative modes based on the outages in a single-cell system. We mathematically derive the outage probability of the AC-NOMA protocol for both the cooperative and noncooperative modes and develop an analytical expression for the overall outage probability by considering the mode adaptation. Through numerical computations, we compare the outage probability of the proposed AC-NOMA protocol to existing protocols, demonstrating its superiority in achieving lower outage probabilities. Furthermore, a threshold-based switching policy is presented to optimize the AC-NOMA protocol efficiently.

This research targets the complex problem of power allocation and scheduling in 5G cellular networks, which operate with Time Division Duplexing technology. To efficiently manage interference between cells, the Dynamic Time Division Duplexing approach was developed. However, changing the operating mode of cells poses significant challenges in optimizing this process. A new algorithm was created, based on an iterative cooperative multi-agent approach, which considers the limitations of cell communication and addresses computational complexity in signal processing. This algorithm operates within a centralized framework, using pytorch, alongside the ACOPF solver, to demonstrate its effectiveness by reducing the drop rate by up to 50% in comparison to traditional scheduling methods.

By utilizing lattice Monte Carlo simulations, the lattice wave function drop method is demonstrated to detect both vacancy lines and vortices in a 2D square lattice Ginzburg-Landau model. The study reveals that in a region of low magnetic field, straight-line segments with a 45-degree angle to the wind direction possess the lowest formation energy, consisting of either a single vacancy line with an energy of 0.43k_BTL or a pair of closely linked vortices with an energy of 0.46k_BTL. As the magnetic field increases, the most stable configuration transforms into a pair of vortices located at a 90-degree angle, with an energy of 2k_BTL. The movement energy of a single vacancy line is found to be 0.48k_BTL, showing a larger value compared to the movement energy of a pair of vortices (0.26k_BTL), which is similar in magnitude to an isolated vortex line (0.27k_BTL), indicating that vacancies tend to pin vortices, hindering their movement. The movement energy of a pair of vortices is found to have a non-linear relationship with the applied magnetic field. The binding energy of a pair of vortices is found to be 0.03k_BTL, with an overlap separation of 6.5 lattice units. The study also reveals that in a region of low magnetic field, the formation energy of a single vacancy

Researchers examined the 2D Ising model under a magnetic field on a Cayley tree to study temperature magnetic phase diagrams and the behavior of normalized cumulants in the pure disorder phase. By altering the disorder pattern, investigators explored whether certain magnetic cumulants could display the same type of scaling seen in lattice-based Ising models. Simulations showed that at the critical temperature, certain normalized cumulants followed the same patterns of dependence on the external magnetic field as corresponding quantities in lattice-based Ising models, with specific symmetries and an asymmetric hysteresis behavior related to parity effects. The investigators found that a specific disorder pattern could eliminate this hysteresis, resulting in more symmetrical behavior. The study also showed that temperature magnetic phase diagrams align with those found using other methods. The work provides a foundation for further study of the 2D Ising model on a Cayley tree, including implications for statistical physics research and potential applications in fields such as materials science.

Researchers who study the properties of matrix product operators in 2-dimensional scenarios can utilize specific 4-dimensional tensors. By examining the underlying structure of these tensors, we found that they can also represent the intersection of two fractal boundaries in a higher-dimensional space, analogous to how certain 2-dimensional tensors describe the intersection of two lines. Our main discovery is that these 4-dimensional tensors are interconnected and can be converted into each other through a combination of symmetries and dualities, much like how 2-dimensional tensors are connected in the ground-state diagram of the Kitaev model. Our findings can inform future studies of matrix product operators by providing a framework that can be used to analyze new, potentially more complex scenarios.

This study demonstrates the potential of Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNNs) to serve as data-driven models for dynamical systems, specifically in a learning framework. We show that an HNN can accurately predict the training dynamics of a system corresponding to data generated by an arbitrary process, without needing the underlying Hamiltonian function. This approach is significant as it sidesteps the challenge of modeling a complex system's dynamics directly. We further illustrate the benefits of an HNN over a LSTM-based meta-learner in this scenario, using the MNIST dataset as an example. The results indicate that an HNN can achieve comparable performance to the meta-learner, but with a more compact model, demonstrating the versatility of Hamiltonian Neural Networks in understanding the world around us.

In the context of a data poisoning attack, a cybercriminal manipulates training data to force machine learning models to produce inaccurate results and undermine user trust. We're developing a robust multi-agent system that utilizes an efficient algorithm to detect and counter poisoning, enabling the training of secure machine learning models. This system comprises an detection agent and a correction agent: the detection agent identifies suspicious training data, while the correction agent creates an improved version of the valid data, leading to a better machine learning model with higher accuracy and trust score.

Airport security screening focuses on detecting prohibited items, a challenging task that requires identifying rare object classes. The standard evaluation protocols for object detection are skewed towards modeling the data distribution of all objects, rather than just the forbidden items. To address this imbalance, we introduce a novel perspective on detecting prohibited items as a meta-task. Since there is no publicly available dataset specifically designed for prohibited items detection, we created HiXray, a high-frequency dataset containing x-ray images with a higher prevalence of items that need to be avoided. Our approach to prohibited items detection employs a hierarchical strategy, dividing the task into main classes and subclass detection. A multi-task framework is then employed for further improvement. By combining two datasets, we developed and evaluated our dataset and approach on the HiXray dataset. The code is available at https://github.com/hi-xray/hi-xray-detection.

Recent research reveals that the polynomial invariant $J_n^T$, initially introduced by the second author, generates invariants for a specific category of links known as torus links. Additionally, the article presents the homogeneous expansion of $J_n^T$ in terms of its underlying variables, as well as its connection to another polynomial invariant known as the Lando-Mumford polynomial. Furthermore, the article establishes a formula for the complete expansion of $J_n^T$, given a set of natural numbers represented by $x_1,\ldots,x_k$, by utilizing the expanded form from a related context.

The primary objective of a deep learning model, operating on text data, is to develop high-quality, human-like data. Despite the utility of data generation methods, constructing coherent entire documents remains a persistent challenge. A widely employed technique, data augmentation, has shown benefits in other NLP applications, such as improving question answering through biased word replacement. This work explores the possibility of enhancing the entire text generation process using data augmentation. Specifically, we investigated the concept of 'latent augmentation,' which involves identifying unremarkable words within a generated sentence and replacing them with new words generated from the language model's own internal representations. Our experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate notable improvements in generated text quality, as measured by both automatic assessments and human feedback. Notably, the benefits of this approach extend beyond the specific models used in this study, as the code and models are openly accessible for further development and integration into commercial products.

This work introduces a novel concept of analyzing the Gamma function and other specific functions from the moment problem, by examining the underlying orthogonal polynomials' behavior along a Hankel curve. By establishing a connection between these functions and the corresponding Szeg\"o kernel, we demonstrate that the Hankel curve's properties dictate the functions' behavior, and conversely, the functions' properties determine the Hankel curve's characteristics. Building upon this relationship, we prove that the Gamma function's representations, including its infinite product form, can be derived from the moment problem's framework. Furthermore, we show that the Gamma function's generalization to negative values can be understood through the orthogonal polynomials generated by the Jacobi operator, when the parameters approach specific limiting values.

The top quark was produced in vast quantities at the LHC, and researchers have precisely measured its creation rate by analyzing data from proton-proton collisions at 8 TeV and 13 TeV. To arrive at these findings, they utilized simulations that incorporated detailed theoretical understanding and accounted for the effects of colliding particles that resulted in similar final states but were not actually connected to the production of top quarks. The analysis revealed a production rate of 177.7 plus or minus 2.8 (8 TeV) and 175.9 plus or minus 1.4 (13 TeV) times the square of the proton's charge, demonstrating a level of precision that surpasses theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics and shows a disparity of 22-31, dependent on energy, and a discrepancy of 1.6-2.5 standard deviations. The investigation further revealed that the majority of top quarks were produced with significant energy, primarily in pairs where the momentum was distributed unevenly, alongside smaller quantities of singular top quarks produced through different mechanisms, albeit with a lesser probability of them being highly energetic.

The accuracy of SQL injection detection can be significantly impacted by the absence of database data, leading to incorrect identification of malicious intent when harmless input is misinterpreted. Existing research has addressed this challenge when database contents are available, but a solution is needed for cases where no data is accessible. To tackle this problem, we present a method that identifies malicious intent in SQL injections without relying on database information, using static analysis of programming language code and dynamic analysis of running applications. By examining the entire input pathway from input validation rules to how data influences application behavior, we can determine the effect of input data despite the absence of database contents. Since this approach accounts for every possible consequence of input data, even without database information, it remains effective. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by successfully identifying malicious intent in a range of scenarios, including both widely used applications and injection tools.

In graph-structured data, a change in three or fewer adjacent data points can result in an infinite number of possible nearby data sets, making it infinitely difficult to determine the adjacent data sets from the definition of differentially private learning. This difficulty complicates the computation of privacy loss in optimized solutions for graph-structured data. We demonstrate that the current methods for computing privacy loss in graph-structured data are impractically slow and may get stuck in infinite loops when working with real-world data sets due to their simplistic approach to checking neighboring data sets. We propose a new approach that uses a more efficient and practical method for computing privacy loss in graph-structured data by checking the nearest data sets based on the structure of the graph rather than individually. This new approach can compute the privacy loss in graph-structured data efficiently, outperforming the current methods by several orders of magnitude, and effectively addressing the infinite loop issue in real-world data sets.

The Euclid mission, set to launch in 2022, will significantly contribute to the understanding of galaxy distributions and the properties of the dark energy that drives galaxy expansion. To effectively analyze its vast data collection, the Euclid Survey Team is developing a series of analytical tools and methodologies. As part of this effort, we're extracting realistic cosmic simulations and transforming the measured flux, shape, and redshift into standard observational quantities. This process, known as 'observationally equivalent' data, enables direct comparison with actual Euclid observations. We're making these data available publicly to facilitate the development of analytical tools and to serve as a benchmark for evaluating Euclid's performance. Additionally, this framework will be crucial for addressing various analytical challenges, including how to combine multi-band data sets and effectively utilize cross-validation techniques.

The development of reliable automated lane keeping systems (AKS) is highly dependent on effectively testing their functionality. Given the impracticality of conducting extensive real-world testing, the use of simulated environments has become a crucial tool in the process. However, simulating human errors that cause failure in the automated system is a significant challenge. One approach to addressing this challenge is to generate flawed road networks that can induce specific types of errors, such as lane changes that trigger a failure in the automated AKS. Unfortunately, existing methods focus on producing general-purpose simulated environments rather than road networks designed to cause specific failures. To address this limitation, this research introduces an innovative approach to generating high-quality simulated road networks with inherent errors that can cause the automated AKS to fail. Building upon established scene synthesis techniques, our proposed framework incorporates a groundbreaking feature selection method inspired by the Mumford Shubik path, enabling the efficient creation of simulated road networks with human-induced errors that can provoke failures in the automated AKS. Moreover, our proposed framework leverages a computational model that complements the feature selection method, enabling the extraction of optimal solution paths that yield superior simulated road networks with minimal computational costs. Ultimately, our research showcases the capability to create exceptionally high-quality simulated road networks with human-induced errors, capable of precipitating failures in the automated AKS, at a fraction of the computational expense compared to existing methods.

The success of music streaming platforms like Spotify and Apple Music is largely due to their ability to provide users with personalized playlists, recommending songs based on their listening habits. This is achieved through collaborative filtering, a technique that identifies patterns in user behavior to make informed recommendations. The accuracy of these predictions relies heavily on a large and diverse user base, but what happens when a new user emerges with little to no data on their listening habits? How can we ensure that they receive high-quality recommendations from the start? This paper presents a novel approach that analyzes the audio content of songs to generate precise recommendations, even for users with limited listening history. By combining acoustic features of music genres with neural networks, we've developed a system that recommends songs based on their acoustic properties, yielding superior results compared to conventional methods.

We present a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic scheme to approximate time evolution in the Euler-Lagrange hydrodynamic scheme, tailored for simulating quantum correlations in lattice models. This new method linearizes the hydrodynamic equations and incorporates a stochastic correction, resulting in an efficient and accurate way to describe non-equilibrium quantum correlations without a knowledge of the interacting Hamiltonian. Notably, our scheme surpasses the performance of existing methods, such as the Lagrange-Gross model and the linearized hydrodynamic scheme, particularly in capturing sudden changes in correlation functions. To demonstrate its efficacy, we apply the linearized stochastic hydrodynamic scheme to a specific example - the Lagrange-Gross model - and compare its results to exact numerical simulations, finding excellent agreement for various correlation functions and different temperatures. Furthermore, our study highlights the benefits of using a hydrodynamic time scale, demonstrating how it can be utilized to anticipate the onset of swift correlation changes without undergoing in-depth computations.

We introduce the Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN), a cutting-edge action proposal network (APN) that leverages a unique dual pathway mechanism to combine visual context information. In DCAN, two parallel streams with distinct field-of-views work together to fuse their results, using inter-stream connections to refine the features and boost the detection accuracy. By implementing a simple yet efficient boundary matching mechanism to guide the proposal refinement, DCAN achieves remarkable performance on the VCOI dataset, surpassing the current state-of-the-art APNs. Our findings are further verified by conducting exhaustive ablation studies and visualizing the internal workings of DCAN through attention heatmap analysis. The code of DCAN has been made publicly available on the Model Zoo of OpenMMLab.

This work provides an in-depth analysis of the palm tree modes observed at the JET tokamak, incorporating edge localized modes and magnetic island interactions, and offers a detailed scenario explaining their origins, which involve the PTMs mentioned earlier.

This research paper presents a novel potential field model that incorporates direction-based characteristics to facilitate more efficient and effective collision avoidance between robots. The traditional repulsive potential field model is reviewed, and then a revised approach is proposed that incorporates the effects of added circular areas around each robot, enabling the prevention of short-range collisions. The modified model includes a new formula for calculating the repulsive potential field values, taking into consideration the orientations and circular cross-sectional areas of the robots. The advantages of the proposed method are highlighted through comparative simulations, demonstrating improved performance in avoiding collisions, especially in scenarios involving rapid changes in motion. The efficient computation of the proposed method is also demonstrated, yielding a practical solution for real-time implementation on robotic platforms.

We establish a new type of large deviation principle for a renewal process operating under its own tail conditions, which enables us to derive a specific standard and easier-to-verify condition. By applying this general result, we obtain specific standard and easier-to-verify conditions that demonstrate how the tail exponent of a power law distribution influences both the renewal process's tail exponent and the probability of observing a particular sequence of letters with a specific frequency in a randomly selected text sample from a memoryless source.

In this research, we analyzed the impact of an intelligent reflecting surface on radar signal performance in scenarios with weak line-of-sight transmission. Mathematically, we characterized the effective radar cross-section in line-of-sight and non-line-of-sight situations. Subsequently, optimization techniques were employed to maximize the radar signal strength when an intelligent reflecting surface is present. Through numerical simulations, we demonstrated the increased sensitivity and accuracy of radar detection in the presence of an intelligent reflecting surface, particularly in non-line-of-sight conditions.

Modern mutation testing is highly beneficial for assessing and comparing testing tools, or fuzzers, which are previously unknown to a program. A strong fuzzer should induce a substantial number of severe program crashes, or SEGVs, through random and unintended input. To effectively evaluate and compare fuzzers, we propose a robust mutation testing framework that simulates extensive program mutations and thoroughly assesses the effectiveness of each fuzzer in discovering program flaws. The proposed framework conducts an exhaustive search for optimal mutation testing strategies and accurately measures the performance of each fuzzer under various testing conditions. Furthermore, our experimental findings reveal the advantages of adaptive mutation testing strategies over less efficient alternative methods and highlight the significant gains realized from employing an optimized search algorithm. The results of our experiments conducted on multiple programs, powered by both cloud and local resources, demonstrate the superior performance of the best fuzzer, as measured by crash densities, often surpasses three times that of the baseline fuzzer.

This proof-of-concept study explores whether a simple, consistent, and robust nearest
mean classifier can match the standards of current continual learning techniques when
using pre-trained models. To achieve this, we conduct a comprehensive set of experiments
on various tasks and models. The findings show that the proposed NM method consistently
achieves comparable performance to the state-of-the-art approaches across all experiments.
The study also highlights the key advantages of using a nearest mean classifier, including
its ease of implementation, computational efficiency, and resistance to performance declines
when handling tasks with significantly differing data sets. The model's ability to model task
relations and distribute knowledge evenly among categories also contributes to its success.
The research utilizes a single-model approach, representing a fundamental case of incremental
learning, and incorporates diverse models, tasks, and scenarios to validate the proposed
approach. The associated code has been made publicly available to facilitate further exploration
of the method's capabilities.

If a manifold $M$ of dimension $n\ge 3$ has a trivial $\pi_2(\tilde M)$, we demonstrate that any map $f:M\to N$ that is close enough to being homotopic to a cover $\tilde f:\tilde M\to N$, results in $\tilde f$ being homotopic to a cover of $f$. This condition holds for all manifolds $M$ in the following cases: when $M$ is a surface, for any map $f:M\to N$; when $M$ is a torus, for any map $f:M\to N$ if $N$ is simply connected; and when $M$ is a lens space, for any map $f:M\to N$ if $N$ is a homology lens space. This research is based on previous findings by Scott and Taylor regarding 4-manifolds.

The paper investigates the dynamics of a specific nonlinear integro-differential equation whose solutions exhibit explosive growth near a stable equilibrium point. The explosive growth can be quantified in terms of the stability of the equilibrium point and a new equation parameter. Additionally, the paper proves the existence of an exponential barrier for a related equation under specific monotonicity conditions and certain boundary restrictions. These findings are relevant to a mathematical model that includes a stochastic component.

The structure of the 64Ni nucleus, specifically its low-lying excitations, has been studied in-depth using a combination of experimental and theoretical methods. Researchers employed relativistic and non-relativistic reaction theories to analyze data from several experiments, and found that the monopole interaction played a key role in shaping the shape of the ground state and its successors. A comparison with other similar nuclei, such as 58Ni and 58Cu, showed that the monopole interaction's effect on the excitation spectrum of these nuclei occurs before a significant gap forms at the N=40 subshell. As a result, the nickel isotopes provide a unique test of the monopole interaction's influence, and have implications for understanding the evolution of shell gaps in this region of the nuclear chart.

We tackle an issue in the context of generalized Lipschitz games, a model that broadens the definition of these games. Specifically, we address a problem posed in an earlier paper, providing a solution for a scenario where players have distinct, game-dependent Lipschitz constants. Our approach demonstrates that a strategy robust to slight changes in an opponent's behavior can indeed flourish in generalized Lipschitz games. Moreover, we establish that this type of game converges to a meaningful equilibrium analysis when players' parameters refine to a single, common value. Notably, this result holds even as the underlying action spaces and payoff functions become increasingly granular. As a key tool, we develop a useful generalization of Delgros' cut function space, which incorporates metric properties.

In the context of evaluating classification models, the reliability of performance metrics is often compromised due to data sampling techniques used in machine learning experiments. To mitigate this issue, a common practice is to employ variance reduction methods for performance estimation. The study presents novel evidence that standard k-fold cross-validation still yields excessively high performance variability, therefore suggesting the adoption of J-k-fold cross-validation for a more stable performance estimate. Through theoretical analysis and empirical validation, the benefits of J-k-fold cross-validation are demonstrated, revealing that it can provide performance metrics with lower variability compared to standard k-fold cross-validation. The proposed method variable k offers optimal performance to a certain data size, thereby facilitating the identification of an optimal k that minimizes variability. The study also establishes the relationship between optimal k and the Fisher information of the sampling method used for performance estimation. The findings suggest that, in comparison to standard k-fold cross-validation, J-k-fold cross-validation reduces performance variability by a factor of two, thereby yielding more reliable performance metrics. The study includes empirical validation across 32 classification datasets, utilizing five distinct machine learning models, demonstrating the effectiveness of J-k-fold cross-validation in minimizing performance variability.

Recent studies have demonstrated that, with the guidance of a pre-trained teacher model, a student model of any depth can match the performance of the teacher, even if the student has significantly fewer parameters. However, the success of this transfer learning heavily relies on the teacher being accurately trained and highly effective. In real-world applications, a model is often trained sequentially, with new data being incorporated into the training process continuously. Therefore, it is impractical to train a teacher model comprehensively before using it to guide a student model. This paper investigates the possibility of using a teacher model that learns from the same dataset as the student model, with the added constraint that the teacher and student models are trained simultaneously. We show that, with a bit more training on the teacher's part, the student model can achieve comparable performance. Moreover, we find that, when the training process is extended to a batch of models, the ability of a teacher model to match the performance of a student model is consistent across all models, provided that the models are trained from scratch simultaneously. Our research offers novel insights into the workings of Teacher-Student architectures, while our findings provide a theoretical basis for the efficient use of teacher models in real-world applications.

Bucket Elimination (BE) is a highly efficient message-passing algorithm for computing the normalized conditional probability distribution in graphical models. BE's impact is magnified when the underlying graph represents a constraint satisfaction problem (CSP). This occurs in CSPs with a bipartite graph, where BE's effectiveness is matched only by its most basic variant. Building on BE's success, our contribution includes two key advancements. Firstly, we improve BE's performance by reducing its computational complexity and, secondly, we offer BE as a fundamental inference method for a broad family of CSPs. Specifically, we propose BE as a method for minimizing an arbitrary submodular function, directly related to CSPs with a min-clone property. This newly identified property bridges the gap between BE and its most basic variant, allowing us to demonstrate BE's equivalence to the latter when the underlying graph represents a min-clique cover. Our results also establish a direct connection between BE and the dual block partitioning method, showing BE to be a special case of the latter. This insight enables us to apply recent dual block partitioning findings to BE, including the detection of fixed points and the solution convergence analysis. Our study first presents an adjustable version of BE and, for the first time, provides a fixed point characterization and convergence guarantee for this broad family of message-passing algorithms.

We've studied a phenomenon where photon absorption is saturated, specifically the frequency shift resulting from photon recoil. By comparing traditional approaches used in atomic physics and opto-atomic systems, we found that the usual assumption of low-saturation photon recoil being negligible may not always hold true, especially in strongly coupled systems with intense light interactions. Our analysis shows that even in highly saturated situations, photon recoil has a significant impact on lineshapes, potently combining with other effects like motional fields and many-body interactions to create intricate spectra patterns. Furthermore, we established an applicable general formula for photon absorption in saturated conditions, taking into consideration the influence of all levels involved, and demonstrated its application to multiple scenarios, including an atomic layer sandwiched between two light fields with varying intensity.

We investigate the exponents characterizing shear jamming in both isotropic and sheared packings of non-bouncing disks with varying friction levels. Contrasting the exponent patterns for frictionless and frictional scenarios indicates distinct scaling relationships between jamming and melting points. Notably, the melting-jamming temperature ratio exhibits linear dependence on the square of the shear modulus near the frictionless shear jamming transition, whereas a cubic relationship is observed for frictional shear jamming. Our findings also reveal that the exponent for the shear modulus's temperature variation generally follows a value of two in both packing types, with only minor deviations due to friction. Additionally, our research confirms that the melting-jamming temperature ratio forms a cohesive continuum with values observed in previous studies of freezing and melting in two-dimensional space.

We derive an explicit formula for the Hilbert-Poincaré series of the centralizer $Z(n)(sl_2)$, and demonstrate that its generating function for each $n$ is a coefficient of the $E_4$ Eisenstein series, closely related to the Eisenstein series $E_4(\tau)$ from elliptic modular forms. Additionally, we establish a connection between the graded dimension of $Z(n)(sl_2)$ and a particular Appell series, and prove that its generating function is compatible with the Atkin-Li algebra.

Lattice and spin-orbit induced Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions in a one-dimensional crystallographic arrangement with non-coplanar magnetic moments can be adjusted through applied magnetic fields. This capability is showcased in a specific 1D magnet, Eu$^{2+}$ doped CoPS$_3$, where DM interactions are modulated in strength, potentially enabling a continuous transition between different magnetic orders. Our theoretical framework predicts that DM interactions undergo an abrupt shift in direction and magnitude due to an inversion in the crystallographic arrangement of interstitial Eu ions, prompting an exploratory experimental search using resonant elastic X-ray scattering at multiple beamlines.

Using a one-dimensional velocity model that accurately captures the essence of a halo moving toward a detector, we contrast the number of Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs) detected by direct methods, including LUX and XENON1D, with their predicted rates. In this one-dimensional scenario, we demonstrate that the velocity distribution of approaching WIMPs is not equivalent to the effective velocity distribution, which is derived from the total halo velocity distribution, including both approaching and receding WIMPs. As a result, the probability density function of incident WIMPs is skewed, with a majority moving at velocities lower than the mean velocity of the halo. Consequently, direct detection experiments, especially those with low thresholds, will more frequently detect incidents with low velocities, which correspond to a specific narrow energy range. Therefore, if such an energy range is used to set limits on these types of particles, those limits will be significantly overestimated, often by a factor of two, when compared to the actual constraints derived from the total halo velocity distribution.

In this study, we examined the underlying algorithms used by major Web search engines to provide results for inquiries relevant to the Australian public sector, with a focus on potential algorithmic bias affecting the outcomes. Our research revealed that algorithms used by Bing, Google, and Yahoo yielded results containing stereotypical racial assumptions in nearly half of the tested searches. We identified twenty-eight subject matters that produced biased results. For example, when searching for information on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples' health, the top-ranked results included information on multiculturalism, multiracial individuals, and racial categories rather than specific, relevant information. Our findings highlighted the need for heightened algorithmic transparency to mitigate the dissemination of harmful stereotypes and misinformation through search engines used by the public.

The potential of a 1.5 TeV, 0.6 TeV, or 1 TeV muon collider to produce various particles at the TeV scale is examined, considering both weak-boson fusion and beam-polished production methods. Investigated particles include vector resonances such as extra $\gamma, Z, W$ bosons, a dark photon, and dark matter pairs produced through a scalar mediator. Calculations account for detector energy cuts, polarization, and systematic uncertainties to provide meaningful sensitivity levels. Compared to weak-boson fusion alone, beam-polished production significantly boosts detection capabilities for certain particles. Certain scenarios, such as extra $Z$ bosons or a dark photon with a mass around 1 TeV, offer distinct production patterns in vector-resonance searches. Additionally, a 1.5 TeV muon collider has the capability to discover extra $\gamma, Z$ bosons or a dark photon if their production cross-section exceeds 10 fb for a polarization of 80%.

We introduce an innovative new way to approximate the behavior of a linear sampling device, called rCASPR, which works by transforming the device's point-spread function into a discrete Fourier transform filter, allowing for efficient computation of its response to any input using the FFT. This simple transformation enables us to easily modify the device's behavior, which can also be adapted to mimic non-linear devices, such as the CMOS image sensor used in the EPR4 camera, by applying its inverse. By utilizing our filter-based approach, we are able to propose a straightforward algorithm to simulate the behavior of the EPR4 camera, which can also be extended to non-linear devices, resulting in an efficient and general-purpose rCASPR simulator that significantly outperforms our previous closed-form expressions in terms of computational speed.

This research paper proposes novel concepts called Inner Critical Core Control Barrier Functions (ICCBFs) and Outer Critical Core Control Barrier Functions (OCCBFs) as an alternative to the use of Higher Order Control Barrier Functions. It provides a new framework for designing robust controllers that can effectively mitigate unknown external forces and ensure the stability of specified core states in nonuniform stability. A key finding demonstrates the equivalence between ICCBFs and higher order CBFs in terms of system applicability, while establishing the advantage of OCCBFs in achieving nonuniform stability without requiring continuous differentiability of the core function. To facilitate implementation, an approximate optimization method is presented for designing both ICCBFs and OCCBFs. The paper also presents a concrete example involving a line following vehicle to illustrate the practical applicability of the proposed framework.

This paper proposes a new topological framework called CF-approximation spaces, 
which serves as a blend between continuous domains and spatial domains. It offers 
an analysis of CF-closed sets within this framework and establishes a categorization 
of indeterminate sets, Scott-closed sets, and Scott-domains as subsets of CF-closed 
sets. Furthermore, it demonstrates that in the context of CF-approximation spaces, 
Scott-domains are equivalent to d-I-domains. This involves showing that every 
d-I-domain can be represented as a subset of a CF-approximation space and that 
every Scott-domain can be embedded isomorphically within a subdomain of any 
given d-I-domain.

This new exact algorithm for paired permutation tests has a significant improvement, with an average speed that is about 100 to 1000 times faster than the previous Monte Carlo approximation, depending on the specific test and dataset. When the number of data points is small, the exact method has a speed advantage, but even with tens of thousands of data points, the exact algorithm remains remarkably efficient, supporting the introduction of an interactive visualization tool. This exact approach uses a novel combination of techniques including the development of a binary tree that is not balanced, hierarchical pruning based on preliminary test results, and the application of dynamic programming to handle pairs of data sets of varying sizes.

This paper uses a game-theoretic model to analyze the collapse of shipping cartels and the resulting fluctuations in freight rates and shipping volumes. Prior research identified a critical period between 2007 and 2015 when shipping cartels suddenly gave up fixed capacity collusions. We develop a stochastic game theory framework to examine the strategic relationships between independent action makers in this industry. Our model shows that the proposed solution satisfies backsteppability, allowing for analysis of smaller-scale games. By solving for the perfect equilibrium in a subgame of individual ship owners, we find that a particular shipping strategy emerges that leads to freight price oscillations and volume fluctuations during the mentioned time period. Furthermore, our model predicts that independent action makers will move towards collusions in times of high freight profit, however this is prevented by the threat of capacity wars. We also identify a control variable that regulates the likelihood of switching between different shipping strategies, influenced by technology advancements, siphoning, and collusions. With this variable modelled, we find that the predicted frequency of strategic switching explains the observed shipping behavior during the studied time period.

We introduce the concept of loom spaces in relation to d-dimensional Delaunay triangulations. Every loom space corresponds to a specific loom configuration and vice versa, indicating a one-to-one correspondence between the two. This connection enables us to explore loom spaces using the geometric properties of Delaunay triangulations. Notably, this framework reveals that locally rigid loom configurations are essentially impossible in 2-dimensional space or above, offering a significant expansion on an earlier one-dimensional proof of unfeasibility.

In the context of graph neural networks, the underlying graph plays a key role in the learning process, and its structure has a significant impact on prediction outcomes. The potential benefits of incorporating additional structural information are particularly evident in classification tasks. To explore this concept, we introduce an innovative approach called graph ratio augmentation, which involves creating diverse synthetic graph topologies from a co-occurrence matrix and combining them with existing node characteristics to form expanded training datasets. Our proposed technique, detailed in the accompanying paper, demonstrates the effectiveness of graph ratio augmentation in relation to regular data augmentation, yielding notable improvements in model generalizability and predictive accuracy on various datasets.

In the context of adaptive non-parametric estimators, a recent finding revealed that conventional approaches to dimensionality reduction are robust in the absence of adaptivity. This research extends those discoveries to include a specific case where the data contains a form of dependence known as an Archimedean copula, ultimately demonstrating that certain adaptive estimators can effectively reduce dimensions independently of whether the data is dependent or independent.

This paper explores recent developments in the field of free boundary minimal surfaces and related geometry topics. Specifically, it presents new examples of compact areas in a broad family of surfaces, likely including many previously unknown instances. These areas are of particular interest because they have a unique property where the boundary intersects the surface in a specific way, making them "singular." A key feature of these surfaces is that they are "minimal," meaning they have the lowest possible area within their given shape. Minimal surfaces play a significant role in geometry and are closely related to various important mathematical concepts, including symplectic geometry and algebraic geometry.

A growing phenomenon in superconductors, where moving magnetic flux lines create entropy in the same magnitude as the vortex core, is being investigated through a proposed model. The suggested vectorized Ginzburg-Landau theory includes a thermal force term, derived from the entropy change of a moving flux line, and is applied to a London-Bose glass model to study the entropy in vortex states. By analyzing the entropy of a single vortex in a honeycomb lattice, the proposed model shows that the London-Bose glass state can reduce the entropy in the vortex core by half. Additionally, the entropy of a moving flux line is found to have the same magnitude as the vortex core, indicating a significant impact on the thermal force. The results further indicate that the entropy in the vortex core can be manipulated through the London-Bose glass state, offering a way to control thermal force and inter-vortex interactions.

A fast and efficient method for an aggregator to share information with a system operator is introduced, utilizing a simple algorithm that can be completed in just one time step. The approach, which is based on the principle of maximum entropy feedback (MEF), allows the operator to effectively manage multiple off/on switching cycles of the aggregator's loads by specifying exactly two parameters: the average power that should be maintained and a safety margin. When implementing MEF, the operator only needs to provide the mean and standard deviation of the target power distribution, making the approach suitable for real-world applications where the system operator needs to respond quickly to changing circumstances. The performance of MEF is evaluated through simulations and compared with established entropy minimization methods, resulting in a better outcome than all of these approaches. The study also pinpoints effective solution strategies for potential vulnerabilities in the approach's design.

Many investors rely on technical analysis to make informed decisions about the future performance of the stock market. This study examines the effectiveness of technical analysis in the Indian stock market by developing a prediction model that combines historical price data and trading volume with various technical indicators. The proposed model is tested on the BSE 500 index components using historical daily stock price data from 2015 to 2021. The results indicate a strong correlation between predicted and actual stock prices, as measured by mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 34.51%. The study employs linear regression analysis to identify the influence of individual technical indicators and stock price characteristics on stock price movement. The findings reveal that certain technical indicators such as relative strength index (RSI) exhibit a significant relationship with stock price movement. The research demonstrates that technical analysis can be an invaluable tool in predicting stock prices.

We've developed three laws of mass loss through the merging of white dwarfs in flight, accounting for how these processes occur as both a supernova and a type of cosmic explosion. We used the LOFAR radio telescope's high sensitivity to identify three instances of dwarf star mergers producing cultural signals. We found that these events occur 8 to 281 times each year that Earth can detect. The majority of these events will take place in dark conditions, with only a small portion being visible as a bright cultural signal. The most common outcome of these mergers is a low-energy gamma burst that can be seen from Earth only 9% of the time. The most powerful of these events, known as a millisecond optical burst, can produce as much light in the optical spectrum as thousands of regular explosions. This research investigates the double Higgs boson production process in the Standard Model Effective Field Theory, using the Higgs Effective Field Theory in a bottom-up approach. We focus on a set of leading operators that contribute significantly to this process and derive constraints on these operators' coefficients using existing LEP, Tevatron, and LHC data, specifically at a center-of-mass energy of 8 TeV, with an integrated luminosity of 19.8 inverse femtobarns in the search for a di-Higgs resonance in the $b\bar b \tau \bar \tau$ final state. We also consider the impact of the double Higgs resonance on the spectrum in the $b\bar b \tau \bar \tau$ channel. We examine the sensitivity of this search to the effective Lagrangian parameters $\kappa_\gamma$ and $\kappa_Z$, and the rescalings of the Higgs self-coupling $\lambda$, and the Yukawa couplings of the Higgs to $b$ and $\tau$ quarks, $y_b$ and $y_\tau$. We find that the current data allow for double Higgs production cross sections at 8 TeV up to 42 pb, 27 pb, 13 pb, and 1.4 pb for $\kappa_\gamma$, $\kappa_Z$, $\lambda$, $y_b$, and $y_\tau$, respectively. We use an unusual coordinate system known as the 'pre-non-relativistic' parametrization, which is based on non-standard and seemingly unrelated time and space coordinates, to achieve an analytical expansion of general relativity. By utilizing this non-standard approach, we can divide the gravitational potential into distinct components related to the non-relativistic and relativistic aspects and demonstrate their separate and combined effects on the motion of mass through relativistic perturbation theory. This method also enables the direct measurement of mass in gravity, which over time results in the curvature of spacetime, a finding consistent with previous research utilizing alternative frameworks. It is also shown in this study that the Thomas precession, present in spin-evolving research, is an integral component of gravity and cannot be removed. It has been mathematically proven that the Thomas precession is an inherent component of gravity and is connected with the proper rotation of mass and its associated gravitational field. It has been found that the Thomas precession causes the curvature of spacetime, leading to further understanding of the intricate relationship between spin, rotation, and gravity.

We investigate a recently proposed variant of the conformal field equations by the authors, which breaks down the fourth order equation into two second order equations, and further simplifies the variational principle. We predict that this alternative framework yields the same general mathematical properties shared by the original Einstein equations. In addition, we develop a computational method to calculate boundary observables for this simplified set of equations, using a specific gauge where the near-boundary behavior of the solutions is well-defined. We demonstrate that the computation results for both the simplified and original equations produce the same values of boundary observables, which can be expressed in terms of the asymptotic charges associated with the gravitational and scalar fields. Notably, the computation can be performed using the simplified equations, which may provide an alternative approach for deriving the asymptotic symmetry group, and further, could be relevant for improving the convergence rate required to compute boundary observables.

We studied the movement of an intruder through granular materials with varying levels of shear stress and flow rates. A cylindrical intruder was moved at different speeds through a transparent granular bed, allowing us to measure the force it exerted and the resulting flow patterns. Our findings revealed that the drag experienced by the intruder follows two distinct patterns, dependent on the flow rate: a lower-force, steady flow at slow speeds and a higher-force, vortex flow at faster speeds. The formation of vortices occurred when the intruder broke through the surface of the granular bed, creating a connection between the two flow types. This phenomenon was influenced by the shear stress of the granular bed and was found to switch between the two flow types at a critical speed that decreases with increasing friction. Any obstacles in the line of sight of the moving intruder can also cause it to switch from the vortex flow to the steady flow, providing a method to achieve the lower-drag steady flow. This research offers a fundamental understanding of the flow of granular materials and may have applications in various industrial settings, such as the transport of solids in pipes filled with granular materials.

Using observations from the ALMA and GMRT, we studied a starburst galaxy, PGG1110+1254, located at a redshift of around 2.5. By analyzing the data, we found that a massive disk galaxy is undergoing intense star formation and has thrown out massive amounts of ionized and neutral gas. These outflows are blocking the galaxy's access to 90% of its cosmic gas supply, forcing the galaxy to rely on the matter it accumulated during its formation. As a result of the outflows, the gas that remains in the galaxy has a depletion time of just 100 million years. Due to the outflows, the galaxy's growth is being significantly slowed, making it harder for it to add more stars. The galaxy's growth is being limited by a combination of outflows, stellar feedback, and a supply chain of gas supply from its host, which is influenced by a massive cluster of galaxies and a web-like structure of gas and matter.

Hybrid architectures for deep learning models have emerged as a viable means to enhance both efficiency and effectiveness. Nonetheless, pinpointing the ideal combination of components that balance performance, memory, and computational demands proves extremely challenging, mainly due to the vast possible configurations, which often exceeds the capacity of batch-size-based optimization techniques. To tackle this issue, we present a novel, scalable algorithm called BoAnon that reduces the search complexity from exponential to linear dependencies on the number of possible configurations. By minimizing a loose bound derived from the actual objective function, BoAnon identifies near-optimal solutions. We demonstrate the superiority of BoAnon over traditional methods, such as the grid search, by successfully applying it to a range of scenarios, including the exploration of hybrid architectures for ResNets, MobileNets, and ShuffleNets, and even combined architectures, which BoAnon finds with orders of magnitude fewer trials.

The ALICE experiment at the LHC has discovered a notable similarity between the transverse momentum dependencies of triangular flow $v_3$ and elliptic flow $v_2$ for various identified particles. To further investigate this finding, the ALICE experiment studied $v_2$ and $v_3$ for pions, kaons, and protons in Xe-Xe collisions at 5.02 TeV. The study revealed that the ratio of $v_3$ to $v_2$ exhibits little dependence on transverse momentum, indicating that the same particle species exhibit the same relative contribution to triangular and elliptic flow across different centrality classifications. Additionally, the experiment discovered that the $v_2$ and $v_3$ ratios for pions, kaons, and protons displayed little variation as a function of transverse momentum, CENTRALITY, or mean number of participants in Xe-Xe collisions.

Large-scale RDF datasets are becoming increasingly popular, due in part to growing usage of Linked Data, yet assessing their quality remains a significant challenge. Existing quality assessment techniques are often tailored to cover a limited number of qualities and are hindered by their inability to take full advantage of descriptive properties. We introduce an innovative approach, called DQA, a comprehensive quality assessment framework for large RDF datasets. This framework, incorporated into a query language called ALCHI, enables the efficient processing of complex queries and the simultaneous computation of diverse quality aspects. We demonstrate the superiority of DQA over established methods in terms of accuracy, versatility, and scalability, achieving substantial enhancements of up to nine times improvement in assessment time. Moreover, DQA exhibits superior data utilization, leveraging descriptive properties to enhance quality assessment. The advancements made possible by DQA are made available through an open-source platform called Lao.

This study explores the performance of minimum density power divergence (MDPDE) and maximum likelihood (MLE) estimators in various dependent process models, including ARMA and Lévy processes, utilizing a combination of theoretical and numerical analysis. The results show the asymptotic properties of both types of estimators, as well as their finite sample properties, which demonstrate the advantages of MDPDE estimators when dealing with only a sample of data. A simulation-based evaluation of the estimators is conducted under dependent conditions, and their performance is analyzed in the context of a continuous-time Lévy process model where the compound sum is observed, rather than the process itself. The findings indicate that the MDPDE can serve as a viable alternative to the maximum likelihood estimator. The associated estimation challenges are addressed through an extension of the Aït-Sahalia- Parkinson method. The research also introduces a new estimator, known as the maximum density power divergence estimator for integrated variations, which yields a more efficient and less volatile estimate of the integrated variation model.

The intense, external influences affecting the gas within active galaxies, until recently undetected, can now be studied thanks to radio and millimeter interferometry. The analysis begins with assuming gas is ionized by shocks originating from the central black hole and surrounding radio source, a theory supported by observations revealing narrow, linear radio sources and massive outflows. A detailed computational model, taking into consideration the effects of shock-ionization, radiative cooling, and gravity, is employed to analyze CGJ 02179−4594, a active galaxy displaying distinctive, linear radio features. By examining various gas properties, the analysis reveals how shock-ionization influences observable characteristics, such as temperatures, which may exceed 10^5 K and exhibit significant gradients, and chemical compositions, which may differ substantially along the length of the radio source. The model also predicts the existence of heavy elements, such as iron, along the length of the radio source, a prediction confirmable through upcoming X-ray observations, and suggests that gas flows are directed towards the southern radio lobe, where conditions are suitable for relativistic electron bremsstrahlung, a phenomenon observable in radio and millimeter data.

The rising popularity of IoT applications with web and mobile interfaces has created a demand for improved testing methodologies beyond traditional techniques. Existing testing tools often struggle to handle complex, modern web applications. We present the Frisbee framework, a novel testing tool designed to streamline the creation and execution of performance and functional tests for modern web and mobile applications. Leveraging a lightweight, headless browser, Frisbee enables the simulation of user interactions and incorporates machine learning algorithms to optimize test data configurations. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through case studies involving real-world applications. The source code of Frisbee is openly accessible on GitHub.

Researchers have calculated the precise rates at which certain particles known as B mesons undergo rare decays, specifically turning into a muon pair. This calculation was performed by analyzing a dataset of collisions collected by the ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider and amounting to 36/fb of data. For the decay process B^0_s to two muons, the experiment's analysis yielded a frequency rate of (8.1 +/- 1.7) x 10^-9, which is in close alignment with the latest theoretical predictions. Furthermore, for the decay process B^0 to two muons, the analysis revealed a rate of (1.0 +/- 0.8) x 10^-9, which is consistent with existing observational data and matches the latest theoretical estimates. Both of these rare decay processes provide valuable insights into aspects of the Standard Model of particle physics.

The development of high-quality 3D models for scenes involving traffic is a challenging task in the field of computer vision. Current approaches to generating these models are often restricted by their reliance on two-dimensional drawings and the absence of an optimized organizational structure for the rendered scenes. To address this, we have developed SceneGen, a novel technique for generating 3D traffic scene models using a hierarchical organization of objects that underpins realistic compositional driving scenarios. Building upon our framework, we have created a large-scale dataset consisting of 10,000 detailed 3D traffic scene models, derived from real-world images captured with a self-driving LiDAR sensor. This dataset serves as both a model repository and a target for our generative model. By combining LiDAR data and SceneGen with deep learning techniques, we have achieved impressive results in modeling these scenes, as evidenced by both human evaluations and metric-based assessments of the generated models' accuracy. Moreover, our method can also be adapted to produce models from a single 2D bird's-eye view image of a traffic scene, thereby enabling the use of ScenesGen for augmenting real-world datasets. Our code, models, and dataset are available for download at https://github.com/daostri/SceneGen.

We establish a direct link between a Cayley tree and the Ising model on any transitive graph, utilizing the graph's automorphism group. This connection allows us to classify the equilibrium states of a Cayley tree using the graph's group representation, and this framework can be extended to the Ising model on any transitive graph.

This research proposes an innovative variant of the Flexible Generalized Minimum Residual method (FGMRES) iteration, aimed at mitigating numerical instability caused by premature degradation of the solution basis within traditional FGMRES implementations. Theoretical convergence properties for the modified iteration are mathematically established, while numerical evidence showcases the method's efficacy in tackling ill-conditioned linear systems and the exponential acceleration it achieves over standard FGMRES in well-conditioned scenarios.

We establish multiple results for ergodic actions on compact groups that further a hypothesis proposed by Giordano, Putnam, and Sofic in 2001.
