Specifically, we demonstrate that for any countable action represented by an array $(G_i)_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$, sharing a common compact subgroup $(H_{ij})_{i,j\in\mathbb{N}}$, there exists an ongoing joint ergodic action $(\pi_{ij})_{i,j\in\mathbb{N}}$ that maintains $(H_{ij})_{i,j\in\mathbb{N}}$ and upholds $(G_i)_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$'s free minimality. This achievement addresses not only open questions concerning Sturmian subshifts but also resolves a long-standing query regarding the sufficiency of relative dynamical systems in maintaining topological free minimal actions.

The formation of massive stars and the associated supernovae can create superbubbles in star-forming regions through which various substances are expelled into the surrounding space. A recent study suggests that the essential constituents of dust observed in the Milky Way's interstellar medium, specifically dust formed in pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae, play a crucial role in shaping superbubbles within massive molecular clouds. Due to the high resolution required to study these regions, the process of superbubble formation has only recently been analyzed with the help of computer simulations. Under certain conditions, the findings indicate that the momentum exchanged between expanding superbubbles and their surroundings can lead to cyclic events lasting millions of years, characterized by periods of star formation and quiescence. As a result of these processes, the distribution of dust and stellar clusters in the galaxy may be influenced by the inherited legacy of massive star clusters. However, the likelihood of detecting these clusters through current surveys is relatively low, about 1 in 300, largely due to their partial dissolution during the superbubble cycle. Therefore, potential candidates for such clusters can be identified by searching for associations of dust and stellar clusters situated near massive molecular clouds and involving a single massive (over 10 times the mass of our sun), relatively old (around 10 million years old) star cluster that has survived its host environment.

We investigate the challenge of detecting three-dimensional objects in images obtained from advanced driver-assistance systems that operate at great distances. The production version of a leading method in this field, known as AutoAirNet, is the subject of this study and is found to be vulnerable to changes in the data it has been trained on. The researchers propose enhancing this method by combining it with techniques that use point clouds obtained from lidar sensors and incorporate the use of additional sensors, such as radar and multi-camera setups. The enhanced version of the model, called MetaAutoAirNet, is shown to excel in predicting the presence of far-distance objects and their exact locations when tested against a rival system known as FC-AIR. The experimental results obtained from training MetaAutoAirNet on a diverse dataset that includes vehicles, pedestrians, and lane markers show that it achieves better performance compared to the baseline method. The researchers also demonstrate the effectiveness of a single-stage detection approach that utilizes a lidar-based depth map in conjunction with RGB images by adapting the model's head to employ a depth map obtained from a lidar sensor and modifying it to integrate the use of additional sensors. The proposed MetaAutoAirNet delivers superior results in far-field 3D detection when compared to the current state-of-the-art methods, outperforming them by a margin of up to 11.3% in terms of performance. The code for MetaAutoAirNet has been made publicly available on a repository that includes the framework's official documentation.

A newly devised quantum machine learning model, based on an entanglement classifier, effectively prepares complex quantum states over a potential energy surface when combined with a classical descriptor. By training an entanglement classifier using a dataset of ground and excited state wavefunctions, the model learns to distinguish entangled electron states from unentangled ones simply by analyzing the electronic density distribution within a low-dimensional space. When this classifier is trained properly, its ability to identify entangled states allows another model, the quantum generator, to replicate these same states even in situations where direct calculation is impractically complex. Testing this approach on a variety of scenarios, including ionized water molecules and sodium dimer photoionization, shows the algorithm can accurately generate excited states that have previously only been accessed through time-consuming direct calculation methods. Notably, one such state, which cannot be reached through conventional means, is now attainable with this model. By bypassing the need for time-consuming direct calculation, this algorithm could potentially expedite the exploration of potential energy surfaces in quantum chemistry, particularly when dealing with multiple-electron systems and complex molecular systems.

During surgery, tracking a virtual 3D model of the patient's organs onto real-time video feed from the operating room can be complicated by the movement and shifting of tissues caused by surgical interventions. To refine this process, we've investigated ways to use machine learning to supplement the traditional method of matching shapes, based on the assumptions that there's some level of noise in the data collected and that the data is partially divided into smaller sections for processing. By using a more efficient algorithm to break down complex structures into their component parts, we've improved the performance of the method and demonstrated that incorporating machine learning into the process yields better results, especially when dealing with larger datasets.

A critical concept in theoretical physics is the energy-momentum tensor, which serves as the basis for conformal mechanics and general relativity. However, most known energy-momentum tensors exhibit specific characteristics that make them non-degenerate. This research seeks to expand the application of these theories to degenerate energy-momentum tensors, while also identifying the specific symmetries within such tensors that can drive second-order differential equations for conformal mechanics and Einstein's general theory of relativity. By doing so, this study aims to demonstrate the equivalence between these driven equations and their first-order nonlinear counterparts. Furthermore, the degenerate nature of these tensors allows for the presence of mass and charge in the resulting physics. Additionally, the associated symmetries give rise to conservation laws, which can be utilized to solve the (semi-)generalized Whittaker problems arising from these non-linear second-order equations.

In the field of self-supervised flow estimation, a promising approach known as mutual suppression has been proposed to counter the negative effects of occlusions. However, the majority of self-supervised flow estimation methods continue to struggle with accurately modeling occlusions, a critical issue that the community requires urgent attention for. This paper introduces an innovative approach called PIFU, a self-supervised flow estimation method that utilizes a bidirectional propagation technique to augment corrupted input images and derive an auxiliary flow field from the unobstructed reconstruction of these images. By employing both forward and backward propagations in a recursive manner, PIFU is capable of diminishing the impact of occlusions by leveraging the contextual information from both the local and distant areas of the input image. Our research is supported by an exhaustive evaluation of seven benchmark datasets, which demonstrates that our proposed method achieves more accurate results in flow estimation in the presence of occlusions, a scenario that mimics real-world scenarios.

Deep learning techniques have significantly impacted the creation of sophisticated classifiers, outperforming conventional approaches in numerous categories. Nevertheless, the high power consumption of deep neural networks (DNNs) poses significant obstacles to their implementation in resource-constrained devices. To overcome these obstacles, this proposal suggests a generalized form of the linear mixed Hamming network (LMN), an efficient and straightforward neural network that matches the performance of advanced neural networks (ANNs) while using lower power. We also introduce a linear Hamming network with an error-correction mechanism that effectively tackles noisy data. In our experiments, our generalized HMN model demonstrates superior performance to existing methods across various classification tasks, outperforming top-performing ANNs by up to 1.5% in accuracy. Additionally, our proposed method achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods on image classification using the Stochastic Hamming Network.

The effects of a strong magnetic field on spin polarized quark matter, specifically regarding its equation of state, are analyzed across various strangeness levels. Formulations of the magnetic field's influence on the quark mass and its potential impact on the quark condensates are examined within the framework of the MIT bag model. As a result, the spin polarized quark matter's response to the magnetic field reveals increased density and deformation for higher strangeness content. Also, the influence of the magnetic field is shown to be magnified at the quark-deconfinement phase transition, potentially allowing for the detection of quark matter via electromagnetic methods in strong magnetic fields.

A notable property of certain cubic graphs, even-2-factorability, is examined in this analysis. Even-2-factorability requires a property where the graph can be divided into two edge-disjoint factors, one even and the other odd, with specific starting points. This study aims to explore the occurrence of even-2-factorability among all cubic graphs, as well as a subclass of these graphs known as the snarks. Additionally, this analysis seeks to identify whether the property of even-2-factorability can be determined efficiently for any given cubic graph. Even-2-factorability is demonstrated to be neither NP-complete nor P-co-NP-complete within the class of cubic graphs, but it is NP-complete within the snarks class. Furthermore, this analysis reveals that the property of even-2-factorability does not have a polynomial verification process among the snarks class.

In our analysis, we'll establish an effective version of a modified Bateman-Horn Conjecture of Li, which has implications for estimating the number of prime values taken by a specific family of quadratic polynomials; these polynomials are of the form $x^2+ax+b$, where $a$ and $b$ are relatively small, non-zero integers. Our primary goal is to demonstrate that for any given positive real number $\Lambda$, the number of prime values of $x^2+ax+b$ within the interval $[1,N]$ is less than $\Lambda \cdot N$ for sufficiently large N. This finding builds upon the work of Li, correcting a technical issue related to the definition of 'low-lying zeros', ensuring that the zeros referred to in the conjecture have a significant impact on the distribution of prime values.

This paper introduces a novel technique called Timeloops, a system call filtering framework that achieves success with interpreted languages like PHP and Python, often considered difficult to secure. Unlike compiled applications, interpreted applications lack a solid barrier against malicious activities as they are transferred from the program to the operating system for execution. Transfers occur every time an application requests an operating system service, often resulting in security breaches. To address this issue, the proposed framework, based on a Linux kernel module, identifies potential vulnerabilities in applications and prevents them from causing harm. The key components of Timeloops are system call filters, monitoring tools, and a static analysis platform. By combining these features, Timeloops can identify system call commands that might lead to security breaches and prevent their execution in real-time, thus enhancing the safety of interpreted applications running on a single core.

Dark matter, if it exhibits Goldstone character, would interact with nucleons at a rate dictated by a symmetry-based mechanism, involving a nonlinear sigma model and a dark su(2) symmetry, and in conjunction with an adjoint field that mediates interactions with other particles. The resulting dark matter-nucleon interactions are computable and self-consistent, and can be derived from an effective field theory of a complex dark matter field, subject to a charge symmetry. The elastic scattering cross-section in this scenario would be expressed in terms of an low-energy parameter, and the associated bound-state problem is manageable within a linear-equation framework. As a result, the elastic scattering cross-section can be determined not just at low energies, but also across all energy ranges, and this applies to both the elastic and inelastic modes of dark matter. The study of the process where a dark matter particle is produced in association with an outgoing nucleon or nucleon system, takes into consideration the internal structure of the dark matter particle and how it influences the effective mass of the outgoing system of nucleons, and takes account of both elastic and inelastic scattering. Finally, the effective field theory of dark matter can also incorporate a non-conserved dark baryon symmetry, and in doing so, it offers a consistent framework for understanding the interactions of dark matter with nucleons and other fields, and for making predictions about the properties of dark matter that can be compared with the findings of direct detection experiments.

Target tracking becomes increasingly complex when some targets remain undetected due to limited or obstructed sensor visibility. This difficulty can be mathematically expressed as a non-convex mixed-integer optimization problem, which is computationally intensive to resolve, especially when targets are numerous. To enhance tracking efficiency, we develop a dynamic dual decomposition approach, dividing the optimization process into more manageable sub-problems that can be solved more quickly. In the short-term context, we use a linearized version of the target detection function, leading to a Convex problem that can be solved rapidly. Our proposed method reduces the computational burden by achieving faster target re-identification compared to existing methods, and our results from a simulation study using a radar tracking scenario demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, with a notable improvement in re-identification time from 432.6 seconds to 11.1 seconds on average.

This study investigates the dynamics of a coupled system that includes a population whose behavior is governed by an infinite number of fully immersed structures, modeled using a nonlinear Kirchhoff type equation. To capture the impact of an external force on the population, the equation includes a term representing an external force with an observability inequality-based dissipation. The analysis focuses on the existence and uniqueness of a weak solution, the existence of a global attractor, and the upper-saturation property of the population when the population's initial observation is limited.

In high-stakes soccer games, players must weigh their options quickly, often in a matter of seconds, when they have the ball in a scoring opportunity. To understand their thought process, we can quantify the expected outcome of each possible action, taking into account the probability of success and the associated rewards and penalties. By modeling player decision-making in this way, we found that certain actions, such as committing a foul or causing the ball to go out, have a similar expected outcome to shooting on goal in certain situations. These findings can inform coaching strategies and provide a framework for analyzing player decisions in the field.

Full waveform inversion (FWI) is a method for enhancing the accuracy of velocity estimates in seismic imaging, though it can be computationally intensive when applied to time-domain data due to the requirement for multiple iterations of forward and inverse processes. One potential alternative is a least-squares formulation that directly optimizes velocity estimates using time-domain wavefields, but this method may be prone to local minima. Another approach, suggested by Holbrook (2017), reformulates the optimization problem in the frequency domain to reduce the computational burden, but it still requires significant CPU time. This paper proposes an additional shortcut to reduce the computational load even further, by using the adjoint method to eliminate the need to store intermediate data, and incorporates the LSQR solver to limit the memory required. The new method is referred to as time-domain least-squares FWI (TDLsFWI). It was tested using synthetic and real-world data sets, and the results indicate that TDLsFWI can recover velocity estimates with similar accuracy to other methods, while requiring substantially less CPU time and memory.

Our investigation reveals that a simple all-optical diode or quasi-circulator design can be achieved by utilizing a chiral interresonator coupling, without requiring an asymmetry in the optical properties of the individual resonators. This technique was applied to a 1D array of dual-mode microtoroid resonators, capable of entering a chiral state due to their spatially symmetrical, non-reciprocal SERS response when exposed to a laser. As a result, all-optical diodes and quasi-circulators function effectively. Furthermore, our findings show that an unusual quasi-circulator configuration can also be created by adding an asymmetry in the optical properties of the resonators, which is made possible by the injection of a forward-traveling light pulse into one of the resonators.

We performed a thorough examination of the 2019 high-energy outburst of the black hole X-ray binary IGR J19294+1816, which took place during the superior conjugant orbit of the system and emerged about 1.5 cycles before the expected high-energy recurrence time. Our analysis of the data from the MAXI, Fermi, Swift, and Chandra space telescopes revealed that the source reached its maximum luminosity of approximately 8.5 x 10 to the 39th erg s to the minus 1 on 2019 September 18. During the outburst, the spectrum exhibited a hard state with a distinct cut-off at about 90 keV and a photon index of around 1.1. Our timing analysis showed that the source generated quasi-periodic brightenings in the 2-11 Hz range, along with a higher frequency hump OCR of approximately 5.8 Hz, which remained consistent throughout the outburst. Additionally, the detection of a mild eccentricity in the OCR and the occurrence of the hump OCR just before the superior conjugant orbit may indicate that the system contains a massive companion star. Our analysis of the outburst also revealed that the system behaved similarly to four other outbursts observed with the High Energy Transient Survey or the MAXI.

We investigate a new type of process called the asymmetric noisy voter model, where individuals can switch between being fully cooperative or fully competitive, and potentially adopt aspects of both. This process takes place on a regular graph and is influenced by the presence of random fluctuations. The goal of this research is to study how the balance between symmetry-breaking aspects and random fluctuations affect the model's behavior. We examine the model's dynamics in the case of a finite number of individuals and a large number of rounds, and our findings also apply to an infinitely large population when time is infinite. We discover that the model can result in three possible outcomes: in some cases, the population will ultimately consist of a single individual; in others, the population will alternate between two fully distinct individuals; and in a third scenario, the population will eventually become a mixture of many different individuals.

Indonesia, being a vast multi-religious country with three main faiths - Islam, Christianity, and Hinduism, particularly in Bali - practices two significant customs that utilize sundials for religious functions. Despite sundials being a vital instrument for measuring time, very few studies have focused on sundials in Indonesia. This study aims to bridge this knowledge gap with a comprehensive analysis of sundials found across the country, incorporating findings from citizen science observations. As observed in the Java Island, sundials exist not just in major cities but also in rural areas and on the islands of Sumatra and Bali, with various forms such as vertical and horizontal sundials used for estimating local time and prayer times. However, it's worth noting that the method used in this study does not involve the calculation of shadow lengths to verify the accuracy of these sundials. With the increasing difficulty in determining local time, especially with the advent of wearable devices that display the universal time, the use of sundials is becoming less necessary. Nonetheless, the cultural and religious significance of sundials in Indonesia demands continued documentation and study, and the involvement of citizen science can play a crucial role in this endeavor.

Our investigation focuses on a dual-purpose system known as DED2D, which combines data and energy sharing between users. To efficiently manage these transfers, we propose and analyze three distinct scheduling strategies, each utilizing different amounts of system information. The first approach, TFIET, allows for flexible meeting of data and energy demands, the second, SISO-STATS, enables single-access, multi-user,, fair data and energy transfers, and the third, MISO-STATS, enables multi-access, multi-user, fair data and energy transfers. Through analytical and numerical investigations of these schemes, particularly in the context of two-dimensional DED2D systems, we determined the minimum amount of system information required to achieve optimal performance and identified fair time fractions and throughput bounds for each scheduling strategy. Our results also highlighted the impact of system parameters, such as the number of users and system dimensions, on the efficiency of these transfers. Ultimately, our findings provide a framework for optimizing data and energy transfers in DED2D systems, with implications for the design of efficient wireless networks that take into account the dual nature of wireless communication resources.

The COVID-19 pandemic has significantly impacted the way people work, causing a shift towards remote working, including in academic environments. In addition to the benefits of increased flexibility, remote working has the added advantage of minimizing in-person meetings. By taking this into consideration, researchers have found ways to automate tasks that were previously conducted manually, such as setting up experimental setups, by leveraging automation tools like Jupyter Notebook, especially in conjunction with Kubernetes. One specific scenario involved the automated setup of an NGSIM traffic simulation using the SUMO and ADO engines. Initially, this process required over an hour to complete manually. By developing a automated process using Jupyter Notebook and Kubernetes, the setup time was reduced to just over 10 minutes, showcasing a significant improvement in efficiency.

We utilized a computational approach based on finite elements to model the behavior of electrostatic phase plates in scanning transmission electron microscopes. By analyzing the effects of varying plate design parameters such as fill-factor and pixel pattern on a 2D grid, we were able to determine how they influence the electron probe size and current density. Through this method, we explored different design options for the phase plates, including the impact of their composition on probe performance, and identified potential limitations of the plates due to their construction from multiple layers of material. We also examined how the behavior of low-voltage probes differs from that of higher-voltage counterparts. By applying this computational framework to a specific microscopes design, we were able to validate our findings against experimental results.

Recent advances in dialogue understanding tasks have seen the success of Dialogue State Tracking (DST) architectures, particularly RNN-based systems, which have achieved notable results. To bridge the gap between sequence-based understanding and planning, we propose a neural framework, called the Conditional Transition Layer (CTL), combining the reliability of RNNs with the efficiency of the transition matrix. To evaluate our approach, we developed a comprehensive evaluation suite consisting of six popular DST benchmarks. Our experiments demonstrate that CTL surpasses state-of-the-art RNN-based models in terms of accuracy, entropy, and F1 score, while also being computationally more efficient. Additionally, a comparative analysis between CTL and the widely-used transformer architecture, specifically the multi-head self-attention mechanism, showed that CTL outperforms the transformer in DST tasks. Our code and models are available for download at https://github.com/leandrogrubisich/Conditional-Transition-Layers.

This research focuses on enhancing loop closure detection in mobile robot applications using deep learning. We propose an attention-based module for a 2D image matching network to prioritize rearrangements in scenes with changes. This module, incorporated into DeepCompare, directly points to the locations in the current image that correspond to changes in the past image, enabling more efficient processing of categories of features that remain the same. Experimental results indicate that the enhanced system is highly effective in identifying loop closures even in environments with significant changes, surpassing competing methods.

The growing popularity of video streaming, coupled with rising mobile data, has created a substantial demand for seamless, high-quality online content access. Ensuring continuous video delivery to meet user demands requires a robust and adaptable approach to maintain performance and quality. A Cloud-based Service Level Agreement model is proposed, designed to minimize costs while upholding quality standards through efficient resource allocation, adaptive re-routing of compromised services, and real-time monitoring. This model leverages the unique benefits of cloud computing, enabling dynamic shifts between available services to maintain performance and quality. Furthermore, a compatible pricing mechanism is proposed to compensate content providers fairly, based on actual service usage. The effectiveness of this model is demonstrated through practical experiments conducted on a simulated virtual environment.

We've developed an in-depth analytical model to describe the quasiparticle behavior at the Fermi level in doped graphene sheets, incorporating the effects of both Coulomb interaction and temperature. This was achieved by modifying the Dirac cone dispersion relationship and integrating out the interactions using a Feynman diagram technique. We found that the renormalized quasiparticle velocity is proportional to the square of the doping level, explicitly defining its relationship as v(k) = v0 * (k/mc). The resulting renormalized velocity then influences the quasiparticle lifetime, lifetime distribution, and single-particle density of states throughout the doped graphene. Consequently, this has a notable impact on quantities such as the specific heat in doped graphene, which exhibits a nonlinear increase with temperature. Our model also highlights the significance of temperature in determining the renormalized velocity and lifetime, and thus must be considered in any comprehensive analysis of doped graphene.

In our approach to automatic speech synthesis, we incorporate the concept of
presumed knowledge from the current and preceding speech segments to achieve
highly natural and engaging delivered content. Unlike conventional methods,
the MaskedSpeech system considers the context of the speech itself, using
self-supervision during training, to effectively utilize speech features up to
400ms of prior audio. Our model utilizes bidirectional connections in both the
encoder and decoder, along with additional bridge modules, to fully
utilize contextual knowledge. We conduct experiments using the LIBRI-TTS dataset
and achieve significant reductions in mean opinion scores (MOS) objective quality
assessment, along with enhanced subjective listener ratings compared to our
baseline. Our results demonstrate substantial gains in the quality and
expressiveness of synthesized speech. Ultimately, the model delivers a level of
performance on par with human narrators in terms of subjective quality and
enjoyment factor.

We investigate the presence of nonlinearly perturbed harmonic oscillators in one-dimensional systems featuring stable solitary waves. Specifically, we analyze the effects of an external periodic force and an adjacent anharmonic oscillator on a particular diatomic chain, the Allen-Cahn equation, and the Klein-Gordon equation. In the case of the diatomic chain and the Allen-Cahn equation, we find that nonlinearly perturbed harmonic oscillators can cause both internal and external orbital stability of solitary waves to fail. Conversely, in the Klein-Gordon equation, we discover that an adjacent anharmonic oscillator can induce anharmonic effects leading to the loss of internal stability of the solitary wave, yet external stability is maintained. Moreover, in all instances, we observe a significant increase in the oscillator frequency due to the presence of the nonlinearly perturbed oscillator, resulting in a substantial amplification of the generated wave amplitude.

Q-balls, a fascinating phenomenon in high-energy physics, possess considerable potential for distinguishing between various fundamental theories. Most analyses of Q-balls are restricted to scenarios with a single stabilising symmetry, despite the presence of multiple such symmetries in many theories. This study ventures beyond this limitation by exploring Q-ball dynamics in models featuring multiple stabilising symmetries, with a particular focus on theories involving both $Z_n$ and $Z_{n+m}$ symmetries. A general framework for identifying the most stable Q-balls has been established, taking into consideration both global minimum and local minimum scenarios. Moreover, an analysis of the conditions necessary for the existence of both $Z_n$ and $Z_{n+m}$ symmetries in theories with abelian gauge fields has been performed, alongside an examination of the potential for both symmetries to be linked with both dark matter and dark energy.

We investigate an intriguing proposal made by Granda and Oliveros that introduces a cosmological constant as a distributed entity, where the cutoff is based on an average distance between particles. We test this concept in a cyclic universe scenario using the holographic principle to determine the lambda term. The effect of the cutoff on the cycle's behavior proves significant, with certain choices resulting in the de Sitter solution being unstable and eventually giving way to a periodic cycle of expansions and contractions. Notably, selecting the cutoff at the Hubble horizon radius prevents the universe from entering the Big Rip phase and makes the universe's current state consistent with observations. Furthermore, the cyclic model can be validated through the magnification of gravitational waves and future tests of the GW150914 signal.

We introduce a novel concept called the L-function of a graph, inspired by the Riemann Hypothesis, and investigate its connections to the properties of a graph's regular covering. As the degree of the covering increases, certain graphs exhibit the desired analytic property of having only non-negative coefficients in their L-series expansion. We demonstrate that this consequence of good complex behavior yields significant benefits in the field of graph theory, particularly in relation to the enumeration of graphs. Moreover, we show that a specific family of graphs, known as hypergraphs, has an inherent connection to the Riemann Hypothesis. This relationship leads to a related conjecture about another family of graphs. Finally, we present an innovative approach to computing the zeta function of a graph based on its L-function.

We establish a connection between the additive Galois module structure of Q extensions that have wild ramification and the representation theory of the absolute Galois group of Q. This connection enables us to conclude that for any finite non-abelian extension K of Q, the representation of the absolute Galois group of K in the linear group L2(3) has a component with wild ramification. Additionally, this component arises from a specific Galois module associated with the extension K, and this module can be expressed as a direct sum of two other Galois modules, each of which is simply connected and generates the Jacobian of the curve defined by y^3 = x - 1, as does their sum.

The research offers a comprehensive investigation into the potential detection of a neutral long-lived particle at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). This investigation considers various production mechanisms and decay modes of the particle, as well as its primary and secondary decay products. Depending on the particle's decay length, different search strategies were employed in the simulation. When the particle's decay length is short, traditional collider detection methods are effective in identifying it. However, for the particle to decay into a stable neutrino, undergo several hadronic interactions before being detected as missing transverse energy, or decompose into two muons with a minimum momentum threshold, special search techniques were necessary. The simulation revealed that, despite being neutral and long-lived, the particle could be found using specialized magnetic detectors that span the length of the LHC apparatus. A neutral long-lived particle with a minimum decay length was found to have less than 1.9 picoseconds of a 2 TeV dimension, and this discovery was made with an integrated luminosity of 300 inverse picobarns, achieved by colliding 10 picobarns of data with each of two beam streams that had opposite neutral charges.

Transformers introduce contextual variances that alter the semantic changes in language sequences, influencing how models perceive word meanings within a sentence. Our research reveals that these contextual variances are unstable and fluctuate depending on sequencing options available, posing an unexpected risk to models that use gradient-based optimization methods to capture semantic shifts. We show that by changing the sequence of a single word, the GlobalSoft and GlobalHard methods significantly misrepresent the degree of semantic change, resulting in inaccurate predictions in downstream tasks. Notably, words with high contextual variances pose an increased threat to these models, especially in low-label-samples settings. Our experiments demonstrate that both the GSoft and GHard methods yield more reliable and less noisy embeddings by minimizing the impact of contextual variances on the sequence of a single word. Moreover, our analysis indicates that the degree of contextual variances correlates with the degree of semantic change, yielding valuable insights for designing more effective neural machine translation models.

A breakthrough analysis of forced oscillation experiments, encompassing NIT-1, NIT-5 and FIP, yields remarkably precise constraints on ultra-light particle properties. These constraints, derived from the inability to detect a forced oscillation signal, result in extremely stringent limits on the ultra-light particle's mass, coupling strength, and the square of a new fundamental parameter $\Lambda$. The parameters $m$, $\Lambda$, and $f_{PL}$ are intimately connected: any variation of $m$ directly affects the ultra-light particle's mass scale $f_{PL}=\sqrt{m\Lambda}$. The research places $m$ within the range of $10^{-23}$ to $10^{-22}$ eV, thereby positioning the ultra-light particle at the upper boundary of the dark matter spectrum. A similar investigation of other dark matter models, such as axions, may lead to a similar conclusion, i.e., the ultra-light particle providing the missing link in our understanding of dark matter, albeit further analysis is needed in those cases.

We develop a detailed model of retinal nucleic acid migration, considering
the intricate distribution of nuclei across the retina, based on recent studies.
We utilize the Drosophila retinal model, which exhibits highly organized and
symmetrical cellular patterns. Our mathematical framework incorporates key
retinal features, such as cell division, the differential adhesion module (DM),
the cell-state switch, and cell positioning mechanisms. We employ a
multi-layer cellular automaton approach to model cell behavior and retinal nucleic
acid migration dynamics. Our simulations successfully replicate the complex,
spatially-organized pattern of retinal nucleic acids observed in live-cell imaging
data. By analyzing our model, we uncover the essential underlying processes that
give rise to the retinal nucleic acid distribution pattern. We also demonstrate
that slight alterations to the DM module can lead to significant changes in the
retinal pattern, highlighting the module's critical role in retinal nucleic acid
migration dynamics.

In compressed sensing, the success of image reconstruction depends heavily on the matrix used for sensing, which requires a low mutual coherence to ensure efficient deconvolution. Forming an efficient sensing matrix with an optimal noise level for compressed sensing is a complex task, especially when coupled with a non-convex optimization problem. We propose an innovative approach to create a compressed sensing system and solve the reconstruction problem, leveraging both artificial intelligence-based image recognition and a mathematical approach to matrix analysis. The designed system includes a matrix with low mutual coherence that facilitates efficient deconvolution and can withstand a specific level of random noise. This system can accurately reconstruct images even in the presence of system errors and noise, significantly reducing the computational burden required for reconstruction. We experiment with the proposed system using a conventional optimization method and one possible approach to deep learning-based optimization, demonstrating its ability to recover compressed images under various forms of compression and noise.

Current scaling theories for active systems near equilibrium are often applied up to five dimensions, but may not hold in higher dimensions due to missing dynamical processes. Using a simple model of actively walking walkers, we find that their collective motion follows a different scaling approach in four-dimensional space. We demonstrate that a more comprehensive hydrodynamic model is needed in this dimension to accurately capture the walkers' behavior. As a result, the walkers' pair-correlation functions exhibit distinct features that cannot be predicted by linearized hydrodynamics. These include out-of-phase correlations that develop over time and long-range fluctuations that are not present in lower dimensions. These findings demonstrate that linearized hydrodynamics is an incomplete description for active systems near equilibrium in some dimensions.

Research institutions rely heavily on email communication, which if breached, poses a significant threat. An established method for detecting breaches involves analyzing an email distribution list's structure and identifying irregularities, but this approach is largely manual and only effective against established threats. In our research, we introduce an innovative automated framework for analyzing email distribution lists and pinpointing potential vulnerabilities. Our proposed model, based on the Graph Neural Network algorithm, successfully identifies potential security breaches in email distribution lists, which our experiments demonstrate can be done with outstanding accuracy and at a reasonable computational cost.

Our theory, grounded in the origin of the van Hove singularity within the cuprate band structure, suggests that an unusual transition in cuprates occurs when the Fermi surface changes shape in a particular way that has a significant impact on the movement of electrons at the critical point and in the surrounding regions. This process causes a sudden shift in the electron interactions and the way they respond to external magnetic fields, resulting in an unexpected combination of effects that can stimulate an abrupt increase in the density of electrons when a magnetic field is applied a certain distance away from the critical point, and also producing a sudden drop in the electronic conductivity when temperature is maintained at a specific point near the transition, all of which are supported by existing data and can only be understood within the context of a specific symmetry of the cuprate materials.

To analyze the Gd-enhanced scintillator solution for measuring neutron flux, a Mark VIa liquid scintillator detector was used to investigate the effectiveness of adding Gadolinium to the solution. By comparing measurements with and without Gd, a significant increase in detection efficiency, up to 16000 counts per second, was found for a particular setting. A mathematical relationship between detection efficiency and neutron energy was derived and showed a good match with existing research. Additionally, a formula to calculate the neutron flux was developed from the results of this study. The validity of this formula was confirmed through independent measurements of neutron flux levels.

This study explores the connection between a limit property of variational functions, modeled using the minimax principle, and the presence of solutions in an equation involving differential inclusion. Specifically, we establish a relationship between the coercive minimization problem and the condition that the graph of a set meets a certain criterion. This relationship is key to proving the validity of an equation involving differential inclusion when the solution set contains an element whose neighborhood intersects with an appropriate class of functions that satisfy a coercivity condition.

A comprehensive analysis of exoplanet systems in reference samples like OPEN and EXO LIFE has revealed a high level of diversity among planetary combinations. To better understand this variety, a new database called EXOPLANET TRANSIT PHOTOMETRY TABLE has been created, containing the combined results of various surveys, with a total of over 1,800 systems and 7,000 objects. By examining the relationships between stellar, planetary, and stellar-planetary properties, it became apparent that certain systems are linked through similar features. For example, systems with small stars often consist of low-mass planets, while those with large stars tend to have more massive planets. Systems sharing certain properties, such as tidal interconnections, have distinct characteristics. Furthermore, certain combinations of planetary masses are underrepresented. Additionally, certain systems are associated with certain types of stellar activity. A classification method can identify the primary characteristics of each system and its place within the database. Systems with similar feature sets exhibit similar combinations of planetary properties, and many share common architectural designs. Many systems exhibit same-same patterns, where similar planetary configurations are linked with similar stellar characteristics. The classification method can also identify systems with unique feature sets that differ from the common designs.

The primary objective of this project is to utilize Natural Language Processing along with Computer Vision to efficiently retrieve information from identification cards, which are present in the Malay language. The ID cards in question belong to Singaporean residents and consist of three types: National Identity Cards, FIN (Work Permit) cards, and Employment Passes. The conventional approach involves manually inspecting and extracting data from these cards using a combination of OCR and manual entry, which is both labor-intensive and prone to errors. To enhance the process, we have developed an optimized pipeline, comprising pre-processing, text extraction using NLP, and subsequent data validation. The ID card-specific models we have trained demonstrate an impressive capacity to accurately classify cards, extract relevant text, and even bypass the need for OCR, as the pre-processing steps alone are sufficient to present the text in a readable format suitable for subsequent analysis. The improved system has shown substantial gains in terms of efficiency, accuracy, and reliability, capable of processing up to 500 cards per hour with minimal errors, largely eliminating the need for human intervention.

The evolution of a quantum system that is continuously influenced by a cyclic variation in energy levels can be understood through the use of coherent states. By applying a periodic change in energy, specific states known as Floquet states are created within the system. Researchers have discovered that, regardless of the intensity of the driving force, dividing the time into segments based on the Rabi period can generate states closely resembling those that would result from continuous, constant driving. This relationship between the systems with periodic and constant driving forces can lead to the development of new technologies, as it could potentially enable the control of fragile coherent states. A new method is presented that allows the precise emulation of the effects of driving forces with distinct periods by combining multiple driving forces with different period lengths. This method holds significant potential in the area of quantum science and could contribute to the creation of durable coherent states required for various applications of quantum technology.

Our team made the notable discovery of three new asteroids, 2015 TT275, 2016 TS4, and 2017 TN8, which orbit around the Sun in a similar plane to the established S5 population. Notably, all three new asteroids share accelerated rotational patterns, indicative of a rotational breakup force that could result from a past collision with a substantial object. Furthermore, their near-infrared spectral characteristics reveal evidence of Xe, O, and C in their compositions, which, when considered alongside their accelerated rotations and S-type main-belt asteroid classifications, suggest these asteroids may possess a composite structure comprising both metallic and stony components. As a result of their discovery habits, all three new asteroids were found at relatively small angular distances of 0.07 radians or below from their intended positions. Utilizing their proposed names, we discuss how the found evidence can lead to the development of enhanced asteroid detection projects, as well as the implications of finding more objects like 2015 TT275, 2016 TS4, and 2017 TN8 in the near future.

Online discussions among communities are changing quickly, with opinions shifting rapidly, even within a short period of time, as seen in online forums and social media. Despite the significance of understanding online community dynamics, especially in the context of political discussions, existing research has a limited scope due to the difficulties associated with collecting large datasets. Typically, existing methods are only effective with small datasets, containing a small number of categories, and have not adequately addressed the challenges of online community evolution, such as the appearance of new topics over time, a lack of assumptions about the structure and formation of discussions, and the absence of models accounting for the evolution of categories and community engagement. To address these shortcomings, we introduce an innovative hierarchical model called the Temporal Latent Hierarchical Topic Model (TLHTM), which builds upon the successes of both the Bag-of-Words model and the Hidden Markov Model. This new model is particularly adept at identifying categories, tracking their usage over time, and modeling online community discussions, even in large datasets, consisting of numerous categories, as seen in online discussions, such as Wikipedia edits or Twitter posts. Moreover, TLHTM is versatile and can be executed on multiple distributed platforms. When tested on two large datasets containing Wikipedia edits and Twitter posts, our proposed model consistently outperforms the existing state-of-the-art methods, such as the Hierarchical Pachinko XML model and the Latent Dirichlet Allocation model, especially when dealing with a larger number of categories, demonstrating its ability

Let $\Gamma$ be a subgroup of $G=PSL_2(\mathbb{R})$ that acts on a compact surface $S$ without fixed points. Assuming that for every open subset $U$ of $S$, the group $\Gamma$ has a subgroup acting continuously, freely, and transitively on the interior of $U$, we will demonstrate that there exists a neighborhood $V$ of $S$ in the space of surfaces, such that for every surface $S'$ within $V$, the group $\Gamma$ acts freely and transitively on the interior of $S'$. Furthermore, this action can be extended to the entire group $G$ on the surface $S'$.

We've created a comprehensive catalog of 81,977 exoplanet candidates by analyzing 20 years of TESS data, and it includes 34,620 new discoveries. To further understand these exoplanet candidates, we developed three separate classifications based on the properties of the host stars. Specifically, we established an M-dwarf mass-radius relation by combining M-dwarf candidates from the SPC and use of the parallaxes to derive a characteristic minimum mass of 0.32M, which helped identify 5,833 exoplanet candidates orbiting M dwarfs. This analysis resulted in 4,203 valid detections of exoplanets in the M-dwarf group. We also developed a category for small-radius stars with masses less than 0.63M and identified 2,786 exoplanet candidates hosted by these low-mass stars. By examining the properties of the stars in our catalog, particularly those with masses less than 0.63M, we found significant discrepancies between the observed population of small-radius stars and the population predicted by theoretical models of stellar evolution and mass function. Our analysis suggests that there may be a population of small, low-mass stars yet undetected as exoplanets, potentially accounting for the discrepancy.

Graphene's unique properties make it suitable for detecting changes in a microenvironment through line waves in the optical and near-ir regions. The efficiency of this detection relies on maintaining a low ohmic loss in the graphene layer. However, this goal is threatened by increasing side leakage currents in large graphene flakes. A critical challenge lies in designing graphene configurations that confine light tightly around defects or edges. This work introduces an innovative approach to the downscaling of graphene, utilizing a periodic array of sub-wavelength patches to control line waves. By adjusting the patch size and shape, we show through finite-element method simulations that edge waves can shift from the optical to the near-ir range. This transformation occurs through a Kohn mode-like transition and can be controlled through the patch's shape and size. The resulting short-wavelength line waves offer more freedom in choosing the photon energy relative to larger graphene flakes. Moreover, the leakage current across the gap between two patches can be minimized by making the patch size comparable to the lattice spacing of carbon atoms in graphene. This design enables a significant reduction in ohmic loss by confining the current within each patch. As a result, the normalized transmission of the line wave mode exhibits exceptionally low loss (less than 10^-3) compared to other graphene configurations. This novel patch-based design may pave the way for innovative applications of graphene, such as enhanced sensing capabilities, by leveraging its unique optical properties.

We tackle the challenge of assessing query tractability in the presence of self-joins by breaking down complex queries into their constituent subqueries, analyzing the relationships between them, and identifying key properties that influence the efficiency of computation. In this context, we've developed a general framework that classifies queries with self-joins as either computationally intractable or manageable by pinpointing specific instances of data alignment. Building upon this framework, we've also established additional criteria for determining the efficiency of queries that incorporate both self-joins and aggregate functions in combination with other operators. Furthermore, our theoretical approach can be applied across various data models, including relational, graph, and semi-structured databases, thereby providing a versatile framework for evaluating query complexity.

Determining whether a given set of polynomial equations has a solution that lies within an given region can be a challenging problem, especially when the equations involve rational functions rather than basic arithmetic operations. While some specific scenarios have achievable solutions, other scenarios, including systems that involve only addition, subtraction, and multiplication, remain insurmountable with current technology. This study shows that deciding the continuity of a rational function-based system, even with relatively simple parameters, is beyond the capabilities of a symbolic computation method and likely requires a random trial approach. The core contribution of this research is to establish that deciding the continuity of a rational function-based system is a problem that falls within the VEQP class, a category of difficult-to-solve problems that can be solved by finding a single counterexample. Additionally, this study provides an example to show that deciding the continuity of a polynomial-based system, even when the system has a specific layout with interconnected components, is also a VEQP class problem.

Using 8.59~fb^-1 of integrated luminosity collected by LHCb at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies, we observe a notable discrepancy in the longitudinal polarization fraction of the decay $\overline{B}^0\to J/\psi K^0_S$, which differs significantly from previously recorded results at the Belle and BaBar experiments. Furthermore, our study indicates a disparity in the longitudinal polarization fractions of the $\overline{B}^0$ and $\overline{B}_s^0$ systems, leading us to conclude a distinct value for the CP-averaged polarization fraction of the $\overline{B}_s^0\to J/\psi K^0_S$ decay, which we have measured as $0.415 \pm 0.024 \pm 0.017$.

Machine learning techniques have recently been successfully integrated with reservoir computing to efficiently model complex dynamic systems. These systems often operate on multiple time scales, making traditional model approaches such as linear differential equations less effective. Our research adapts a nonlinear delay line reservoir computer to simulate two intricate systems: a dual-time scale laser system and an chaotic macroscopic magnetic pendulum. By comparing the computer's output against a high-resolution simulation of these systems, we demonstrate the efficacy of the approach. A key finding reveals that the nonlinear reservoir computer is remarkably efficient at modeling systems with significant time scale disparities, even when trained with highly granular data. In contrast to traditional models, it requires minimal prior knowledge of the system's dynamics and scale structure, making it particularly suited for analyzing poorly understood processes.

We develop a novel estimator that offers a bias-corrected prediction of the squared error of bias-reduced estimators, such as those created using the method of controls, doubly robust estimators, and inverse probability weighted estimators. Our estimator is particularly effective in situations where the estimators in question have a specific form of smoothness. We can establish the consistency of our estimator under typically assumed conditions and confirm that it achieves the minimum possible error rate of consistency. To obtain estimates in practice, we suggest a straightforward approach based on a Taylor series expansion that is computationally efficient. We provide an empirical illustration utilizing both simulated and real-world data.

We have investigated how feedback control can contribute to estimating the reachable state sets of a dynamic system within a given time frame. By systematically analyzing linear time-invariant systems, we have determined a method to compute the minimum number of states required to predict the system's behavior. This approach enables us to design and optimize a discrete state estimator using optimal control theory. Furthermore, we have established that a stabilizable system can be controlled to any desired stable equilibrium point.

Our investigation reveals that the exponential increase in computational cost associated with an exponential growth in signal dimensions can be mitigated by employing local functionals that are inherently two-dimensional. We demonstrate that for Euclidean data featuring linear underlying structures, our proposed method using local representation achieves comparable performance to the baseline model using global representation on high-dimensional data, significantly outperforming the baseline on low-dimensional data. Additionally, our technique exhibits a notable boost in generalization performance, particularly for signals below 5 dimensions, where our model with global representation struggles. We validate our findings through a range of dimensions, corroborated by the decay of the spectral radius of the kernel matrix as a key factor enabling success with low-dimensional data.

The animacy of an object can be determined by various factors including its visual characteristics and mechanical properties. Yet, the relationships between these factors and the object's place on the animacy spectrum remain unclear. We propose that an object's animacy is a continuous trait, influenced by how easily it can be categorized visually and its ability to move independently. These factors have a significant impact on people's interactions with the object, with effects seen on brain regions associated with emotion, language, and motor function. We used a non-verbal pointing task to study how objects move and are perceived when they have their own movement, are pushed, or fall. The results showed that objects that could move independently were seen as more animate than those that required external forces to move, and were also better at evoking strong emotions and suggestions of purpose. When reaching for these objects, the movement of goal objects and obstacles influenced motor planning, with objects that could move independently causing the most overlap in brain activity between vision and action.

This study examines the behavior of zeros for automorphic L-functions by analyzing the L-functions of holomorphic and imholomorphic cusp forms, GL(2) L-functions, and their connections to Landau-Siegel zeros. By developing the concept of zero repulsion, we demonstrate that extensive families of automorphic L-functions exhibit zero avoidance, indicating that landau-siegel zeros are unlikely to exist. This conclusion is also confirmed by computational data. Additionally, zero repulsion is shown to occur among L-functions within each family of elliptic curves over the rational numbers, enforcing a significant gap between the lower bounds of zeros for these L-functions and the estimated values according to the conjectured behavior of zeros for these L-functions.

This paper develops a relational Hoare logic for quantum programs, using a novel approach that combines Hoare theory with program relational verification. By assigning a quantitative measure to the relationship between inputs and outputs from Hoare's qualitative analysis, we have created a framework that can effectively tackle the challenges of quantum program verification. This new logic, called QHRL, has been successfully demonstrated through a set of notable examples, including a quantum version of the binary search algorithm, a blocking queue developed by Michael and Scott, and the Shor algorithm for factoring numbers with a certain property, all of which have been formally proved correct using QHRL.

We develop a new spatial epidemic model that integrates multiple factors: 
counter-intuitive super-spreader behavior, where one individual can cause countless infections, 
airborne transmission within a confined space with varying levels of contamination, 
distinct sub-populations with separate dynamics, and the impact of wearing a mask on 
infection probability. This comprehensive approach accounts for the significant impact 
one or more super-spreader events can have on the overall infection rate in a closed setting, 
demonstrating how such outbreaks rapidly lead to widespread outbreaks many times over. 
In contrast, standard non-spatial epidemic models typically underestimate the peak infection 
rate by a significant margin. Our model also incorporates the effect of immunity on infection 
dynamics, which can result in persistent infections if the recovery rate is slower than the 
infection rate among immune individuals, or even if the population remains entirely immune. 
Furthermore, our model shows that the presence of a vaccine can substantially reduce the 
peak infection rate, often by a major order of magnitude, and can also accelerate the 
convergence towards the steady-state infection rate. Our findings are validated through 
numerical simulations, which provide valuable insights into the complex interplay between 
spatial transmission, super-spreader events, and the coexistence of different sub-populations.

Let's consider a power series $\sum_{n=0}^\infty A_n(t)$ of operators from a given Banach space to a Hilbert space, where $\{A_n(t)\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}_0}$ forms a $C_0$-semigroup for each fixed $t\in\mathbb{R}$. We can view this as an operator-valued power series, denoted by $\sum_{n=0}^\infty A_n(t)$. The main objective of our research is to investigate the convergence, codiskcyclicity, and representation of this operator-valued power series within the space of codifferentiable functions, provided that certain conditions are met.

The quality of solar vector magnetic field maps is not entirely representative if all areas are given equal weight, as currently standard inversion techniques do. This is because they fail to differentiate between filled magnetic areas (where magnetic field is present) and empty areas (where it is not). This problem becomes especially significant in regions with high interconnectivity, where small amounts of magnetic field can make a considerable difference in the overall picture. To accurately assess the fill fraction of magnetic fields, we have incorporated an optimization technique that accounts for the cross-correlation of observables across the solar surface. This method takes the length of line-of-sight path into consideration and produces more reliable results, especially in regions with high interconnectivity. By applying this technique to observations from the Helioseismic and Magnetic Instrument of the Solar Maximum Mission during the X1.0 flare on 2014 February 14, we found significant areas with low fill fraction (less than 50%) in regions associated with the flare, suggesting that weak magnetic fields observed across the solar surface may have a significant role in the onset of major solar flares.

We analyzed a comprehensive sample of 284 star clusters younger than 7 billion years that are located in a specific region of the Milky Way, situated near the solar neighborhood. Observations from four different infrared surveys - VVV, VHS, and LSST - were combined to study the present-day properties of these clusters. A detailed examination of the surface density of a vertical column within the solar neighborhood revealed a notable increase in cluster density as time progresses. However, when limiting the scope to the solar neighborhood, we did not observe a similar enhancement in cluster density within a horizontal plane. Furthermore, we classified clusters into four distinct age groups and compared their horizontal and vertical densities, only to find that densities within a horizontal plane follow a similar pattern of growth across all cluster ages. This phenomenon was initially reported in 2013. As time progresses from 1 to 7 billion years, the cluster density within a vertical column continues to exhibit higher rates of growth than within a horizontal plane. As a result, differences in density within these frames of reference continue to widen over time. We formulated rate parameters for dispersion and saturation of cluster distribution within a horizontal plane, with rates of $0.76\pm0.07\times(0.78\pm0.08)$ kpc$^{1.5}$ billion years$^{-1}$ and a saturation point of approximately 13.5 billion years. Additionally, models of cluster distribution were compared to predictions of the galaxy's potential, with a particular

To calculate the decay width of unstable particles in lattice QCD, a new approach has been proposed that builds on previous methods by incorporating a complex pole into the two-point function. The suggested technique specifically addresses finite-volume effects that arise from lattice simulations. By analyzing the dispersion relation associated with the complex pole, the decay width can be determined from the imaginary part of the finite-volume spectral function, without needing to invoke the lattice sum over infinite modes of the propagator. Instead, the real part of the finite-volume spectral function, which reflects the oscillatory spectral structure seen in lattice simulations, serves as the volume-independent probe of the decay width. The accuracy of this method was verified through a lattice study of the tau lepton decay to a kaon, and the calculated hadronic width for this process was found to be in line with the expected value based on chiral perturbation theory. The method has the benefit of not needing a fit to the exponential off-shell signal in the two-point function, which can become distorted by finite lattice spacings, particularly in cases of heavier particles.

We introduce an efficient novel method for affine parameter coupling that may be used in various Monte Carlo techniques. The proposed method involves complex-valued layers in the form of a generalised complex conjugate layer which has the benefit of significantly reducing the required number of forward passes. This leads to a significant improvement in the responsiveness of our approach to changes in the affine parameters. The method is an improvement over the conventional coupling method which typically relies on real-valued layers and slow parameter updates. The efficiency of our approach is particularly evident in situations involving multiple Markov chains, where the benefit of increased responsiveness can be leveraged to reduce the overall number of required forward passes. The simplicity and effectiveness of our approach make it an attractive solution for a broad range of stochastic computation tasks. The code for our approach has been thoroughly evaluated on a range of benchmark functions and Noisy Intermediate Scale Model (NISM) evaluations, and the findings are accompanied by a comprehensive theoretical analysis of the method's efficiency.

We derive a precise asymptotic count for the number of integers, denoted as $y(f_x)$, that are $y$-friable, where $x$ and $y$ are large and satisfying the ratio $\frac{\log x}{\log y}$ equaling some value $\theta$. Under the Riemann Hypothesis, we establish that the count of $y$-friable integers, denoted as $\pi(x,y)$, can be expressed as approximately $x\frac{\pi^2}{6(\log x/\log y)^2}$ for $\theta$ equaling any fixed non-zero value. Additionally, we establish an upper bound for the variance of $\pi(x,y)$, where the bound is shown to be $\frac{x}{\log x}\frac{1}{(\log x/\log y)^2}$ under the Riemann Hypothesis, and this upper bound is found to be similar in magnitude to the square of the mean value of $\pi(x,y)$.

This paper investigates how topological entropy is affected when a recognizable mapping is applied to a subshift of finite type. Specifically, we prove that topological entropy after applying a recognizable mapping to a subshift of finite type is equal to the supremum of the topological entropy of recurrent orbits under that mapping. This result is key to showing that topological entropy is continuous when restricted to recognizable mappings that have no fixed points, by linking it to the study of recurrent orbits. Additionally, this research relates topological entropy to the complexity of subshifts when considering recognizable mappings that have no fixed points, and can be one-to-one elsewhere.

Most current pre-training methods for language models rely on generating contradictory or related text but solely utilize the self-correction of models through contrastive learning. This typically requires supervised data and model fine-tuning. In contrast, our research introduces an unsupervised technique called ReCross that leverages the differences models make when presented with the same input in varying forms, such as identical sentences with slight alterations and semantically equivalent sentences. By combining two learning approaches (contrastive learning and regularization), ReCross enhances the consistency of these models on various tasks, such as sentiment analysis and question-answering, without the need for labeled data. In fact, our findings show that even without fine-tuning, our model enhancements lead to significant improvements, averaging 8% better performance across 11 evaluation datasets compared to the baseline models.

This study introduces the m-ar-K function, a variant of the arithmetical kth nearest neighbor (ar-K) distance method. The proposed method is compared to alternative dimensionality reduction techniques, including multi-dimensional scaling, Sammon's mapping, and linear discriminant analysis. A set of statistical measures is utilized to evaluate the results, revealing that the m-ar-K function achieves comparable or superior performance to these established methods in various scenarios.

In the gaming sector, requirements engineering research is particularly underdeveloped.
Despite the escalating costs of developing modern computer games, the field of requirements engineering (RE) has thus far received scant attention.
To stimulate progress in this area, we present an overview of the gaming industry, its financials, and the role of RE within it.
In addition, we outline key research opportunities and potential solutions, while highlighting the potential benefits of integrating RE principles into the development cycle of video games.

Due to rising data protection regulations, there's a growing need for models that can be safely tuned without exposing private data. This requirement rules out conventional optimization techniques, which necessitate accessing the training data multiple times. To address this challenge, we've developed a method for hyperparameter selection that minimizes the necessary data access while ensuring no disclosure of sensitive information. By treating the optimal hyperparameters as a function of the model's performance, which can be estimated using public data, we transform the problem into a task of function estimation. We leverage this perspective to design a hyperparameter selection framework that incorporates the model's variability, thereby preventing overfitting when estimating the optimal hyperparameters. Moreover, our approach conforms to a privacy standard, which ensures that the necessary data access meets a predetermined security benchmark. We've also devised a way to adapt the optimal hyperparameters for a model that incorporates a learning variable, which can be applied to deep learning models. Notably, our method outperforms alternative private hyperparameter selection methods in experiments conducted across multiple domains.

In this study, we demonstrate that a specific configuration of spheres within a geometric shape called a wedge, which is derived from a Coxeter group, requires a minimum number of spheres that is directly proportional to the size of a sub-set of generators from which the Coxeter group is constructed. This finding specifically shows that if a sub-set of generators from which the Coxeter group is constructed has 'k' elements, then a corresponding wedge will feature at least as many spheres as there are elements in a group of size 'n.k', where 'n' represents the number of dimensions and "k" is a whole number. We further assert that if a wedge with the same geometric structure as another wedge with 'k' generators also has the capability of containing at least as many spheres as there are elements in a group of size 'n.k', then those two wedges are equivalent in geometric structure. We utilize this new geometric understanding of spheres within wedges to establish the completeness of certain polynomial equations derived from the Coxeter group, by utilizing the findings of mathematicians who have contributed to the resolution of similar problems.

The accurate assessment of detector systems, specifically those related to astronomical observations, involves measuring the amount of light passing through a device and quantifying its variability. However, these measurements are compromised when the detector is subjected to correlated technical fluctuations, or ``electronic noise.'' The impact of such noise can be significant, especially when analyzing faint sources, as seen in a published study on the measurement of the Hubble constant using Cepheid variables in the Milky Way. The research was conducted using the VLT's K2 camera and discovered that it was susceptible to two types of noise: image sensor temperature fluctuations and mechanical residuals from the telescope's lens. The study found that the camera's ability to accurately measure brightness was off track by assuming uncorrelated noise, which led to an overestimation of its uncertainty by up to 10 times. The investigation developed a new method to account for noise correlations, which can be applied to other sensitive detector systems, and is particularly useful when dealing with sensitive measurements of small, variable sources. The technique was particularly effective in resolving the uncertainty related to optical interferometry measurements of exoplanets, which could have a significant impact on research in this area.

The HERBS spectrograph on the XSHB telescope at the Declination Switching Infrared Telescope will allow for the spectroscopic analysis of stars, particularly those in the Galactic bulge, using the new instrument. To test the spectrographic performance, a setup consisting of a NIST-certified calibration unit, a fiber link, and the spectrograph itself was employed in a series of measurements. These tests revealed the presence of a systematic error, estimated at -35 km/s, in the velocity measurements, which can be corrected with a simple model. A more comprehensive assessment of residual abundances was conducted to ensure the instrument's accuracy in this regard. The results indicate that HERBS can provide reliable relative abundances with an accuracy of better than 0.1 dex and a scatter of less than 0.05 dex. Furthermore, the instrument is capable of detecting velocity patterns (stellar spectra variations over time) and may contribute to the detection of stellar oscillations similar to those found in the Sun.

In multiple peak rumor propagation scenarios, initial spreaders hold significant peaks of attention, contributing (peaking between 5-10 days) to the main peak. However, the impact of their actions is temporary. Our mathematical model reveals that precursor features and location-based information facilitate rumors reaching 90% of the population in 6.53 days, as opposed to 13.43 days without this information. Higher attitude values among spreaders accelerate peak arrival and intensify peak amplitude. Our simulation demonstrates that targeted interventions aimed at early adopters, based on their behavior and geographical position, can effectively mitigate peak amplitude and acceleration.

Using data on Fornax cluster planetary nebulae, a complete sample was compiled to calculate the cluster's distance. The analysis involved the planetary nebulae luminosity function, which was found to be statistically consistent with the parameters of a cluster with a typical density distribution. The distance to the cluster was then determined to be 3.99 billion parsecs with an uncertainty of 0.13 billion parsecs, or an error of 3.3 million parsecs. Additionally, the most recent measurements of the Hubble constant were used to calculate the cluster's velocity dispersion at 157 kilometers per second, or about 96,000 miles per second. Images from the Hubble Space Telescope were used to select potential planetary nebulae candidates, resulting in the discovery of 272 new planetary nebulae in the Fornax cluster. Of these, 107 were confirmed through the observation of their spectra. The study's sample of planetary nebanae, consisting of 282 objects, was found to be sufficient for calculating the cluster's size using the Virial Method. The size of the cluster was determined to be 3.1 degrees in diameter, or about 7.5 times the angle of a Full Moon.

Every day, numerous users visit streaming services like social media and online platforms, generating a massive amount of data in real-time. To make informed decisions, develop new features, and prevent user harassment, these services need fast, automated detection of users' activities and characteristics from this data. Traditional machine learning methods are slow to handle data streams, making them unsuitable for this task. In response, researchers have developed a rapid machine learning framework based on a data-driven approach, transforming the method into a fully automated process. To achieve this, we created a novel, automated system for feature construction, which uses logical rules to extract actionable insights from data streams. Under normal operating conditions, our system yields outcomes comparable to those of finely tuned, optimized numerical libraries used in static data settings. To overcome challenges posed by unusual or critical situations, we incorporated an adaptive subsystem for feature construction, which can prioritize existing dimensions for reprocessing to produce new, valuable insights quickly. In critical circumstances, our system accelerates feature construction without delay, trading off marginal accuracy for speed. We put a streamlined version of our automated feature construction framework to the test on a data stream generated by the Google Knowledge Graph, a massive static dataset, and several real-world data streams.
